## Aspect Medical Systems (industry, United States)

**Nassib G. Chamoun** — engineer; founder of Aspect Medical Systems and primary inventor of the Bispectral Index (BIS)

Nassib Chamoun trained as an electrical and computer engineer, earning a BS from Northeastern University and an MS from Boston University, and worked as a fellow in cardiovascular physiology at the Lown Cardiovascular Laboratory at the Harvard School of Public Health before founding Aspect Medical Systems in 1987 in Newton, Massachusetts. He is the primary inventor of the Bispectral Index (BIS), a processed-EEG variable built on bispectral — that is, higher-order spectral — analysis, which quantifies the phase coupling among EEG frequency components in addition to the power information used by conventional spectral descriptors. Jeffrey Sigl and Chamoun laid out the methodological basis of that approach in 1994. The FDA cleared BIS in 1996 as a measure of the effects of anesthetics and sedatives on the brain, and a further clearance in 2003 addressed its use in guiding anesthetic administration to reduce awareness with recall. Under Chamoun as president and chief executive, Aspect grew into a publicly traded company and BIS became the most widely used depth-of-anesthesia monitor.

The contribution that matters most for pharmacodynamic modeling is that BIS supplied a continuous, bounded scalar measure of hypnotic drug effect that could be linked directly to modeled effect-site concentration. Chamoun was a co-author of the 1997 study — led by Valérie Billard with Pedro Gambús, Donald Stanski, and Steven Shafer of the Stanford/Palo Alto group — that compared spectral edge frequency, relative delta power, and BIS as EEG measures of alfentanil, propofol, and midazolam effect. Relating each descriptor to estimated effect-site concentrations, the investigators found that the measures yielded broadly comparable estimates of drug potency and of plasma–effect-site equilibration for the hypnotics, and concluded that bispectral analysis can serve as a measure of the EEG effects of anesthetic drugs. That validation, together with volunteer studies such as those of Peter Glass and colleagues, helped establish BIS as a standard pharmacodynamic endpoint for hypnotics — it is the effect measure underlying widely used propofol PK/PD models, including the general-purpose Eleveld model applied in target-controlled infusion.

Chamoun's work on risk prediction from administrative data produced the Risk Stratification Index, published with Daniel Sessler and colleagues in 2010. After Covidien acquired Aspect Medical Systems in 2009 he served as vice president for technology, research, and clinical development, and he subsequently founded the Health Data Analytics Institute, where he is president and chief executive officer.

*Key references:* Sigl JC, Chamoun NG. An introduction to bispectral analysis for the electroencephalogram. J Clin Monit. 1994;10(6):392–404. • Billard V, Gambus PL, Chamoun N, Stanski DR, Shafer SL. A comparison of spectral edge, delta power, and bispectral index as EEG measures of alfentanil, propofol, and midazolam drug effect. Clin Pharmacol Ther. 1997;61(1):45–58.

## Bonn & Erlangen (Germany)

**Jürgen Schüttler** — anesthesiologist; propofol and opioid pharmacokinetics/pharmacodynamics, population PK, and closed-loop anesthesia (University of Bonn, then chair at Erlangen)

Schüttler is one of the central figures in intravenous anesthetic PK/PD. With Schwilden and Stoeckel in Bonn he co-developed and validated EEG-driven closed-loop control of intravenous anesthetics and helped translate compartmental modeling into practical model-based infusion, collaborating with Donald Stanski's group in Palo Alto on EEG measures of hypnotic drug effect, including the pharmacodynamic modeling of ketamine and its enantiomers. His most widely cited contribution is a large multicenter population pharmacokinetic analysis of propofol (with Harald Ihmsen), which quantified the influence of age, weight, and mode of administration on propofol disposition using a three-compartment model — parameters that became one of the standard reference population models for propofol, alongside the Marsh, Schnider and Eleveld models implemented in commercial TCI pumps. Across his career he also characterized the PK/PD of opioids (e.g., alfentanil, fentanyl) and their interaction with hypnotics, contributing to the response-surface understanding of anesthetic drug combinations.

*Key reference:* Schüttler J, Ihmsen H. Population pharmacokinetics of propofol: a multicenter study. Anesthesiology. 2000;92(3):727–738.

---

**Helmut Schwilden** — anesthesiologist and clinical pharmacologist; pioneer of EEG-guided, model-based, and closed-loop intravenous anesthesia

Schwilden laid much of the quantitative groundwork for target-controlled infusion (TCI) and feedback-controlled anesthesia. His 1981 paper derived a general algorithm for computing the dosing regimen needed to reach and hold a desired drug concentration in any compartment of a linear pharmacokinetic model — the generalization, building on Krüger-Thiemer's and Vaughan and Tucker's multicompartment infusion mathematics, that underlies the "BET" (bolus–elimination–transfer) schemes used in the Bonn CATIA system and later TCI. He then pursued the electroencephalogram (EEG) as a real-time pharmacodynamic measure of anesthetic drug effect, championing the median EEG frequency as the controlled variable. Working with Horst Stoeckel and Jürgen Schüttler in Bonn, he built and clinically tested adaptive closed-loop systems that titrated methohexital and propofol to a target median EEG frequency, the first closed-loop general-anesthesia systems in humans driven by an explicit pharmacokinetic–pharmacodynamic model (EEG servo-control of anesthesia itself dates to Bickford in 1950). This EEG-and-pharmacokinetics program applied the effect-site/ke0 framework of Hull and of Sheiner and Stanski to link plasma concentration to a continuously measurable CNS effect.

*Key references:* Schwilden H. A general method for calculating the dosage scheme in linear pharmacokinetics. Eur J Clin Pharmacol. 1981;20(5):379–386. • Schwilden H, Stoeckel H, Schüttler J. Closed-loop feedback control of propofol anaesthesia by quantitative EEG analysis in humans. Br J Anaesth. 1989;62(3):290–296.

## Duke University

**Tong Joo "T.J." Gan** — anesthesiologist and clinical investigator; BIS-guided titration of intravenous anesthesia, antiemetic pharmacology, and enhanced recovery (Duke University, later Stony Brook and MD Anderson)

T.J. Gan rose through the academic ranks at Duke University Medical Center, where he served as vice chair for clinical research and faculty development and collaborated with Peter S. A. Glass on the clinical pharmacology of intravenous anesthesia. He was first author of a multicenter trial that demonstrated the clinical value of titrating a hypnotic to a processed-EEG measure of drug effect. In 302 patients at four institutions anesthetized with propofol, alfentanil, and nitrous oxide, adjusting the propofol infusion to a target bispectral index of 45–60 — rather than to standard clinical signs alone — reduced propofol administration, shortened time to extubation, and left more patients oriented on arrival in the recovery room and eligible for earlier discharge. Carl E. Rosow and Peter Sebel, who appear elsewhere in this panel, were among the co-authors. The trial is a direct clinical demonstration of the premise behind concentration-targeted dosing: that hypnotic delivery is best steered by a measure of effect rather than by a fixed weight-based dose.

Gan's Duke work also produced a concentration–effect result obtained with the target-controlled machinery this program simulates. Using a computer-assisted continuous infusion device to hold propofol at target plasma concentrations of 100, 200, 400, and 800 ng/mL in patients already nauseated or vomiting in the recovery room, he and Glass, with Ginsberg and colleagues, identified a median plasma concentration of about 343 ng/mL associated with an antiemetic response, and translated it into practical dosing — roughly a 10 mg bolus followed by an infusion near 10 µg·kg⁻¹·min⁻¹. The study was small and open-label, but it illustrates how a targeted concentration, rather than a bolus dose, can be the clinically meaningful quantity.

He subsequently chaired the Department of Anesthesiology at Stony Brook University's Renaissance School of Medicine from 2014 to 2022, and then became division head of Anesthesiology, Critical Care and Pain Medicine at the University of Texas MD Anderson Cancer Center. Gan is the lead author of successive international consensus guidelines on postoperative nausea and vomiting, including the fourth guidelines in 2020 and the executive summary of the fifth in 2025; these define the risk-stratification and multimodal prophylaxis framework in routine perioperative use. Much of his later work concerns enhanced recovery after surgery (ERAS) and perioperative outcomes.

*Key references:* Gan TJ, Glass PS, Windsor A, Payne F, Rosow C, Sebel P, Manberg P. Bispectral index monitoring allows faster emergence and improved recovery from propofol, alfentanil, and nitrous oxide anesthesia. Anesthesiology. 1997;87(4):808–815. • Gan TJ, Belani KG, Bergese S, et al. Fourth consensus guidelines for the management of postoperative nausea and vomiting. Anesth Analg. 2020;131(2):411–448.

**Peter S. A. Glass** — anesthesiologist and clinical pharmacologist; leader in target-controlled infusion research (Duke University, later Stony Brook)

Peter Glass is a leading clinical investigator of target-controlled infusion and of the pharmacology of short-acting anesthetic agents. He directed influential first-in-human and validation studies characterizing the pharmacokinetics and pharmacodynamics of the ultra-short-acting opioid remifentanil, and he contributed extensively to the clinical validation of propofol and opioid TCI. His volunteer and surgical studies helped define the concentration–effect relationships that underpin practical target-controlled dosing.

Glass also co-authored the work that named the "context-sensitive half-time," based on the simulations of Shafer and Varvel — a naming that reshaped how anesthesiologists reason about drug offset after continuous infusion. His body of work bridged rigorous PK/PD modeling and everyday clinical dosing decisions.

*Key reference:* Glass PSA, Hardman D, Kamiyama Y, Quill TJ, Marton G, Donn KH, Grosse CM, Hermann D. Preliminary pharmacokinetics and pharmacodynamics of an ultra-short-acting opioid: remifentanil (GI87084B). Anesth Analg. 1993;77(5):1031–1040.

---

**James R. Jacobs** — biomedical engineer; developer of TCI control algorithms and co-author of the paper that named the context-sensitive half-time

James Jacobs made foundational engineering contributions to model-driven drug delivery in anesthesia. He derived an analytically optimal control algorithm for driving a pharmacokinetic model to a physician-specified target concentration, a formulation that made real-time, interactively adjustable target-controlled infusion practical and that was implemented in the Duke CACI II infusion system; his later effect-site algorithm, developed with E. A. Williams, was in turn adopted by research TCI programs such as STELPUMP and IVFEED. Delete the sentence. The paragraph then ends: "...his later effect-site algorithm, developed with E. A. Williams, was in turn adopted by research TCI programs such as STELPUMP and IVFEED."

With Michael Hughes and Peter Glass, Jacobs named the context-sensitive half-time — the time for drug concentration to fall by 50% after stopping an infusion of a given duration. The underlying result was not new: it was a subset of the simulations published by Shafer and Varvel, which had already shown that the traditional elimination half-life poorly predicts recovery after anesthetic infusions. What Hughes, Glass and Jacobs contributed was to simplify that work and give it a name, and the name is what carried the idea into everyday clinical reasoning about drug offset.

*Key references:* Jacobs JR. Algorithm for optimal linear model-based control with application to pharmacokinetic model-driven drug delivery. IEEE Trans Biomed Eng. 1990;37(1):107–109. • Shafer SL, Varvel JR. Pharmacokinetics, pharmacodynamics, and rational opioid selection. Anesthesiology. 1991;74(1):53–63. • Hughes MA, Glass PSA, Jacobs JR. Context-sensitive half-time in multicompartment pharmacokinetic models for intravenous anesthetic drugs. Anesthesiology. 1992;76(3):334–341.

**Evan D. Kharasch** — anesthesiologist and clinical pharmacologist, Duke University; methadone and anesthetic drug metabolism, pharmacogenetics, and drug interactions

Evan D. Kharasch is the Merel H. Harmel Distinguished Professor of Anesthesiology at Duke University School of Medicine. He previously held faculty appointments at the University of Washington in Seattle and at Washington University in St. Louis, where he was the Russell D. and Mary B. Shelden Professor of Anesthesiology and founding director of the Center for Clinical Pharmacology. He served as Editor-in-Chief of *Anesthesiology* from 2016 until 2023.

Kharasch is the principal authority on the clinical pharmacokinetics of **methadone**, a drug whose long and highly variable half-life makes it one of the hardest opioids to dose rationally. Working with Christine Hoffer, Dale Whittington, and Pamela Sheffels, he used pupillary miosis as a pharmacodynamic measure alongside plasma concentrations to separate the hepatic and intestinal contributions of CYP3A to methadone disposition. That work showed that intestinal and hepatic CYP3A activity has no significant effect on methadone concentrations, clearance, or clinical effects, overturning the prevailing assumption that CYP3A4 governs methadone clearance and pointing instead to **CYP2B6**; his subsequent work established CYP2B6 as the principal determinant and showed that it acts stereoselectively, preferentially metabolizing the S-enantiomer while the active R-enantiomer accumulates. He extended this to the clinical consequences: CYP2B6 genetic variants and inducers or inhibitors (including antiretrovirals) shift methadone clearance severalfold, which explains much of the interindividual variability in methadone effect and a substantial share of its disproportionate role in opioid-related deaths. Because a compartmental simulation is only as good as its clearance estimate and the covariates that modify it, this body of work supplies the mechanistic explanation for why methadone parameters vary so widely between patients.

His earlier research established the enzymatic basis of volatile anesthetic biotransformation. With Kenneth Thummel he identified cytochrome P450 2E1 as the predominant human hepatic enzyme catalyzing oxidative defluorination of sevoflurane, isoflurane, and methoxyflurane — the reaction that liberates inorganic fluoride and had long been implicated in methoxyflurane nephrotoxicity. He extended this to renal metabolism and to the fate of compound A, the sevoflurane degradation product formed in carbon dioxide absorbents, characterizing its glutathione- and β-lyase-dependent bioactivation and arguing, from the species differences in that pathway, that the proximal tubular injury seen in rats does not translate to patients — a position he has defended in a contested literature. Parallel work identified the P450 isoforms responsible for ketamine N-demethylation to norketamine and the effect of CYP2B6 variants on stereoselective ketamine metabolism.

*Key references:* Kharasch ED, Thummel KE. Identification of cytochrome P450 2E1 as the predominant enzyme catalyzing human liver microsomal defluorination of sevoflurane, isoflurane, and methoxyflurane. Anesthesiology. 1993;79(4):795–807. • Kharasch ED, Hoffer C, Whittington D, Sheffels P. Role of hepatic and intestinal cytochrome P450 3A and 2B6 in the metabolism, disposition, and miotic effects of methadone. Clin Pharmacol Ther. 2004;76(3):250–269.

**J. Gerald "Jerry" Reves** — cardiac anesthesiologist; chair of anesthesiology at Duke, later dean of the College of Medicine at the Medical University of South Carolina (MUSC)

Jerry Reves was a pioneer of modern cardiac anesthesia and a central mentor of the group that developed computer-assisted continuous infusion (CACI) at Alabama and its successor, CACI II, at Duke. Trained at MUSC and the University of Alabama at Birmingham, he built the cardiac anesthesia division at Duke University, chaired the Department of Anesthesiology there (1991–2001), and served as dean and vice president for medical affairs at MUSC (2001–2010). His research established much of the clinical pharmacology of the benzodiazepine midazolam in anesthesia and advanced the understanding of opioid (fentanyl) pharmacokinetics during cardiac surgery.

Working with engineer J. Michael Alvis, Reves led the University of Alabama at Birmingham effort that translated three-compartment pharmacokinetic models into a bedside infusion controller, producing the landmark 1985 demonstration that a computer-driven infusion could hold plasma fentanyl close to a chosen target (measured/predicted ratios of 0.99 and 1.08) and that, in its variable-target mode, it gave greater hemodynamic stability and required fewer adjuvant drug interventions than manual bolus dosing. This work is a direct forerunner of contemporary target-controlled infusion (TCI) systems.

*Key references:* Reves JG, Fragen RJ, Vinik HR, Greenblatt DJ. Midazolam: pharmacology and uses. Anesthesiology. 1985;62(3):310–324. • Alvis JM, Reves JG, Govier AV, et al. Computer-assisted continuous infusions of fentanyl during cardiac anesthesia: comparison with a manual method. Anesthesiology. 1985;63(1):41–49.

## Emory University

**James M. Bailey** — anesthesiologist and PK/PD modeler; context-sensitive/decrement times and closed-loop control (Emory University; later Northeast Georgia)

Bailey applied rigorous pharmacokinetic/pharmacodynamic modeling and simulation to questions of anesthetic onset and recovery. He is closely associated with the "context-sensitive half-time" concept — the time for drug concentration to fall 50% after stopping an infusion of a given duration — named for intravenous drugs by Hughes, Glass, and Jacobs, based on the work of Shafer and Varvel. Bailey extended the idea to the inhaled anesthetics, using computer simulation to compute context-sensitive half-times and other decrement times (80%, 90%) for enflurane, isoflurane, sevoflurane, and desflurane — showing that the 50% decrement times are uniformly short (<5 min) and barely lengthen with duration, and that the agents separate only in the deeper 80% and 90% decrement times that actually govern emergence. He also contributed to model-based and closed-loop drug delivery and to the general methodology of quantifying the time course of anesthetic drug effect.

*Key references:* Shafer SL, Varvel JR. Pharmacokinetics, pharmacodynamics, and rational opioid selection. Anesthesiology. 1991;74(1):53–63. • Hughes MA, Glass PSA, Jacobs JR. Context-sensitive half-time in multicompartment pharmacokinetic models for intravenous anesthetic drugs. Anesthesiology. 1992;76(3):334–341. • Bailey JM. Context-sensitive half-times and other decrement times of inhaled anesthetics. Anesth Analg. 1997;85(3):681–686.

**Carl C. Hug Jr.** — anesthesiologist and pharmacologist, Emory University School of Medicine; clinical pharmacology of the anesthetic opioids (fentanyl, alfentanil) and opioid concentration–effect relationships

Carl Hug was a leading academic authority on the clinical pharmacology of the synthetic opioids used in anesthesia, particularly fentanyl and alfentanil. Holding both an MD and a PhD in pharmacology, he devoted more than five decades to anesthesiology research and education at Emory. His studies helped establish the plasma concentration–effect relationships of opioids during surgery and the concept of alfentanil as a "kinetically predictable" analgesic well suited to infusion-based dosing.

Among his most cited work, the study with Ausems, Stanski, and Burm defined the plasma alfentanil concentrations required to blunt responses to specific surgical stimuli (intubation, incision, closure) during nitrous oxide anesthesia — data that directly informed rational opioid infusion regimens and TCI targets. Hug also held major leadership roles, serving as president of the American Board of Anesthesiology (1992–1993) and of the Foundation for Anesthesia Education and Research (1998–2001). Carl Hug passed away in 2022.

*Key reference:* Ausems ME, Hug CC Jr, Stanski DR, Burm AGL. Plasma concentrations of alfentanil required to supplement nitrous oxide anesthesia for general surgery. Anesthesiology. 1986;65(4):362–373.

---

**Peter S. Sebel** — anesthesiologist, Emory University School of Medicine; opioid pharmacokinetics, EEG and bispectral index measures of anesthetic drug effect, and intraoperative awareness

Sebel took his qualifying medical degree in the United Kingdom (King's College Hospital Medical School, University of London) and subsequently earned a doctorate for research in anesthetic pharmacology. His early work was conducted with James G. Bovill on the clinical pharmacology of the synthetic opioids in cardiac anesthesia. Their 1980 study of high-dose fentanyl was an early pharmacokinetic description of the drug at anesthetic doses, characterizing the rapid initial distribution and prolonged terminal phase and documenting the abrupt fall in plasma concentration produced by hemodilution on cardiopulmonary bypass. Bovill and Sebel then joined those kinetics to a quantitative measure of drug effect, using the processed electroencephalogram to track opioid action in high-dose fentanyl anesthesia and in high-dose alfentanil anesthesia, where the EEG changes were explicitly correlated with measured plasma concentrations. This concentration–EEG work belongs to the body of research that established the EEG as a continuous, graded pharmacodynamic endpoint for intravenous anesthetics.

At Emory, Sebel became a central figure in the development and validation of the bispectral index. He was first author of the 1997 multicenter study of bispectral EEG analysis for monitoring anesthetic effect, a co-author with Peter S. A. Glass, Carl E. Rosow, and colleagues on the companion volunteer study relating BIS to sedation and memory across propofol, midazolam, isoflurane, and alfentanil, and a co-author with Tong Joo Gan and Glass on the BIS Utility Study Group trial showing faster emergence and improved recovery when anesthetic delivery was titrated to BIS. Taken together, these studies treated the index as a drug-effect measure that could be related to concentration and titrated against it, rather than merely a monitor display.

Sebel later led one of the largest prospective American investigations of intraoperative awareness. The 2004 multicenter United States study reported data from 19,575 patients across seven academic centers with structured postoperative interviews, and found an incidence of definite awareness of about 0.13% — a benchmark figure that framed subsequent debate over whether EEG-based depth-of-anesthesia monitoring reduces awareness.

*Key references:* Bovill JG, Sebel PS. Pharmacokinetics of high-dose fentanyl: a study in patients undergoing cardiac surgery. Br J Anaesth. 1980;52(8):795–801. • Sebel PS, Bowdle TA, Ghoneim MM, Rampil IJ, Padilla RE, Gan TJ, et al. The incidence of awareness during anesthesia: a multicenter United States study. Anesth Analg. 2004;99(3):833–839.

## Food and Drug Administration (FDA)

**Carl C. Peck** — physician and clinical pharmacologist; first Director of the FDA Center for Drug Evaluation and Research (CDER), 1987–1993; founder of the Center for Drug Development Science

Carl Peck is among the most influential advocates for quantitative, model-based drug development and for embedding pharmacokinetic/pharmacodynamic (PK/PD) and exposure-response reasoning into regulatory decision-making. Trained in internal medicine and clinical pharmacology, he directed the Division of Clinical Pharmacology at the Uniformed Services University of the Health Sciences (1980–1987) before becoming the first Director of CDER when the FDA split its drug and biologics centers in 1987, and he led CDER until his retirement from government service in 1993.

At and after the FDA, Peck argued that drug development should be a structured, quantitative learning process rather than a series of isolated trials. Working alongside Lewis B. Sheiner and other pioneers of population PK/PD, he helped popularize the "learn and confirm" paradigm and pushed for exposure-response analysis, population modeling, and simulation as tools for dose selection and labeling — the same modeling tradition that underlies target-controlled infusion (TCI) and PK/PD models for anesthetics. In 1994 he founded the Center for Drug Development Science (CDDS) at Georgetown University Medical Center, later affiliated with the UCSF School of Pharmacy. He received the ASCPT Sheiner–Beal Pharmacometrics Award in 2017.

*Key reference:* Peck CC, Barr WH, Benet LZ, et al. Opportunities for integration of pharmacokinetics, pharmacodynamics, and toxicokinetics in rational drug development. Pharm Res. 1992;9(6):826–833.

---

**Daniel A. Spyker** — physician-engineer (PhD, MD) and pharmacokineticist; academic clinical pharmacology (University of Virginia), later FDA medical officer (CDER)

Daniel Spyker combines formal quantitative training with clinical medicine: a PhD in electrical engineering and mathematics and an MD, with board certifications in internal medicine, medical toxicology, and clinical pharmacology. For roughly a decade he served on the internal-medicine faculty in the Division of Clinical Pharmacology at the University of Virginia, where he helped build the Blue Ridge Poison Center and applied compartmental modeling and Bayesian pharmacokinetic methods to dosing and poisoning problems — bridging rigorous PK analysis with clinical toxicology and poison-control practice.

His early research produced quantitative pharmacokinetic studies of antibiotics, including dose-dependent (nonlinear) absorption rate of amoxicillin after oral and intramuscular dosing, benchmarked against intravenous administration (total absorption itself was dose-independent) — work still cited in modern analyses of amoxicillin absorption kinetics. He later served as a Medical Officer in FDA's CDER (Pilot Drug Evaluation Staff), contributing to pharmacokinetics, exposure-response, and dose/exposure evaluation in the review setting, and subsequently worked in the Center for Devices and Radiological Health (CDRH). His career reflects the same emphasis on quantitative clinical pharmacology and model-based analysis that characterizes the PK/PD tradition used in anesthetic simulation.

*Key reference:* Spyker DA, Rugloski RJ, Vann RL, O'Brien WM. Pharmacokinetics of amoxicillin: dose dependence after intravenous, oral, and intramuscular administration. Antimicrob Agents Chemother. 1977;11(1):132–141.

## Ghent University & Demed Engineering (Belgium)

**Tom De Smet** — biomedical engineer; developer of the RUGLOOP / RUGLOOP II TCI and closed-loop software; founder of Demed Engineering, Temse (Belgium)

De Smet is the biomedical engineer who, with Michel Struys at Ghent University, built the RUGLOOP modular TCI and closed-loop software (later versions RUGLOOP II and RugloopII Waves) that underpinned much of the Ghent group's TCI and automated-anesthesia research. The software captured physiologic monitor data and implemented both open-loop TCI and BIS-guided closed-loop control of propofol. He owns Demed Engineering, the Temse firm named in his publication affiliations, and is a co-owner of the RUGLOOP software.

His methodological contributions include simulation-based performance evaluation of closed-loop controllers and the development of a Bayesian-based, patient-individualized adaptive control method for BIS-guided propofol delivery, validated for clinical feasibility.

*Key reference:* De Smet T, Struys MMRF, Neckebroek MM, Van den Hauwe K, Bonte S, Mortier EP. The accuracy and clinical feasibility of a new bayesian-based closed-loop control system for propofol administration using the bispectral index as a controlled variable. Anesth Analg. 2008;107(4):1200–1210.

## Harvard Medical School (MGH & Brigham and Women's Hospital, Boston)

**James H. Philip** — anesthesiologist and bioengineer, Brigham and Women's Hospital; author of the "Gas Man" simulation

James H. Philip is an anesthesiologist and bioengineer who created "Gas Man," the widely used educational program that simulates the uptake and distribution of inhaled anesthetics. Gas Man depicts, pictorially and graphically, the movement of anesthetic gas and vapor from the vaporizer through the breathing circuit, lungs, blood, and tissues to the site of action in the brain and spinal cord, and models agents including halothane, enflurane, isoflurane, desflurane, sevoflurane, nitrous oxide, xenon, and ether. First developed in the 1980s and refined over decades, it remains a standard teaching tool for inhalation-anesthesia kinetics.

Philip's broader contributions span anesthesia pharmacokinetic simulation, gas and vapor monitoring, and clinical instrumentation. He worked directly with the bioengineer Daniel Raemer, who appears elsewhere in this panel, in the Department of Anesthesia at Brigham and Women's Hospital, co-authoring studies on capnography and on the design of anesthesia monitoring arrays; Raemer's model-driven alfentanil infusion work was carried out in that same department.

*Key reference:* Philip JH. Gas Man — an example of goal-oriented computer-assisted teaching which results in learning. Int J Clin Monit Comput. 1986;3(3):165–173.

---

**Daniel B. Raemer** — biomedical engineer, Brigham and Women's Hospital, later Massachusetts General Hospital; gas monitoring, model-driven infusion, and anesthesia simulation

Dan Raemer is a bioengineer (PhD) whose early work centered on respiratory gas monitoring and capnography and on the instrumentation and control of drug delivery. He was a key contributor to model-driven (target-controlled) drug infusion, applying population pharmacokinetics prospectively to computer-controlled infusion pumps so that a desired plasma or effect-site concentration could be targeted rather than a fixed infusion rate — a foundational validation for the class of tools that simulators like stanpumpR embody. This work was carried out with S. L. Shafer, J. R. Varvel, and colleagues.

In the second phase of his career Raemer became a central figure in the professionalization of healthcare simulation. In 1995 he left his post as Director of Clinical Engineering at Brigham and Women's Hospital to join the Boston Anesthesia Simulation Center (created by Jeffrey Cooper in 1993), where as a founding trustee he built the clinical programs that led to its renaming as the Center for Medical Simulation, and he served as the founding president of the Society for Simulation in Healthcare (2005). He held appointments as a bioengineer at MGH and Associate Professor of Anaesthesia at Harvard Medical School.

*Key reference:* Raemer DB, Buschman A, Varvel JR, Philip BK, Johnson MD, Stein DA, Shafer SL. The prospective use of population pharmacokinetics in a computer-driven infusion system for alfentanil. Anesthesiology. 1990;73(1):66–72.

**Carl E. Rosow** — anesthesiologist and pharmacologist, Massachusetts General Hospital

Carl Rosow was a clinician-scientist who bridged anesthesiology and pharmacology, holding both an MD and a PhD in pharmacology (Boston University). For over three decades at MGH and Harvard Medical School he taught anesthetic pharmacology and conducted clinical studies of opioid pharmacodynamics and pharmacokinetics. His early work on opioid-induced histamine release helped explain the hemodynamic differences among morphine, fentanyl, and related agents, informing safer intraoperative opioid use.

## Hôpital Bichat–Claude Bernard (Paris, France)

**Frédérique Servin** — anesthesiologist, Département d'Anesthésie-Réanimation, Hôpital Bichat–Claude Bernard (AP-HP), Paris; propofol pharmacokinetics in special populations and TCI

Frédérique Servin is a French anesthesiologist known for her pharmacokinetic characterization of propofol in special populations and for her work on total intravenous anesthesia (TIVA) and target-controlled infusion (TCI). In an influential 1988 study she and colleagues described the pharmacokinetics and protein binding of propofol in patients with hepatic cirrhosis, showing that overall disposition and protein binding were largely preserved despite liver disease — an early demonstration relevant to dosing propofol in patients with impaired hepatic function. She subsequently examined propofol infusion for maintenance of anesthesia in morbidly obese patients, providing pharmacokinetic and recovery data that became a standard reference for scaling propofol dosing to body weight in obesity and that continues to inform TCI dosing models.

Across her career Servin has contributed to the clinical pharmacology of intravenous anesthetics, TCI implementation, and dosing in challenging populations, and remains an active contributor to the European intravenous-anesthesia and TCI literature.

*Key references:* Servin F, Desmonts JM, Haberer JP, Cockshott ID, Plummer GF, Farinotti R. Pharmacokinetics and protein binding of propofol in patients with cirrhosis. Anesthesiology. 1988;69(6):887–891. • Servin F, Farinotti R, Haberer JP, Desmonts JM. Propofol infusion for maintenance of anesthesia in morbidly obese patients receiving nitrous oxide. A clinical and pharmacokinetic study. Anesthesiology. 1993;78(4):657–665.

## ICI / Zeneca / AstraZeneca (industry, United Kingdom)

**John Baird "Iain" Glen** — veterinarian and pharmacologist; discoverer of propofol (Diprivan) and leader of the Diprifusor TCI program

Glen — a Scottish veterinary surgeon by training, who publishes as J. B. Glen but is universally known as "Iain" — identified propofol (2,6-diisopropylphenol) as an anesthetic while working at Imperial Chemical Industries beginning in the early 1970s, and led its development into the clinically used formulation Diprivan. He subsequently coordinated the development of the "Diprifusor," the first commercial target-controlled infusion system for propofol, including assessment of delivery performance and collaboration with pump manufacturers. For the discovery and development of propofol he received the 2018 Lasker–DeBakey Clinical Medical Research Award.

*Key reference:* Glen JB. The development of 'Diprifusor': a TCI system for propofol. Anaesthesia. 1998;53(Suppl 1):13–21.

---

**David B. Goodale** — clinical development scientist, ICI / Zeneca / AstraZeneca (propofol program)

David B. Goodale is a neuropharmacologist (PhD) who also holds a DDS and residency training in hospital anesthesia, and who spent more than two decades in clinical development and medical affairs at ICI Pharmaceuticals and its successors Zeneca and AstraZeneca — the company that developed and marketed propofol (Diprivan) — latterly as US executive clinical director for the Diprivan program. — the company that developed and marketed propofol (Diprivan). In that role he collaborated with academic investigators, including the Stanford group and its Bern collaborators, on the clinical pharmacology of intravenous anesthetics. He is a co-author on the Schnider propofol pharmacokinetic study, contributing the industry/development perspective to a study that became a foundation for propofol target-controlled infusion, and he is likewise a co-author of the companion analysis of the same volunteer dataset, which defined the influence of age on propofol pharmacodynamics.

*Key references:* Schnider TW, Minto CF, Gambus PL, Andresen C, Goodale DB, Shafer SL, Youngs EJ. The influence of method of administration and covariates on the pharmacokinetics of propofol in adult volunteers. Anesthesiology. 1998;88(5):1170–1182. • Schnider TW, Minto CF, Shafer SL, Gambus PL, Andresen C, Goodale DB, Youngs EJ. The influence of age on propofol pharmacodynamics. Anesthesiology. 1999;90(6):1502–1516.

## Leiden University Medical Center (Netherlands)

**Max Ausems** — anesthesiologist; alfentanil pharmacokinetics/pharmacodynamics and model-based ("computer-assisted") infusion

Ausems carried out foundational work defining the plasma alfentanil concentrations required to supplement nitrous oxide anesthesia and to suppress responses to specific surgical stimuli, translating opioid effect into concentration targets that could be actively controlled. This research was a direct precursor to modern target-controlled infusion (TCI): it established the concentration–effect relationships that a model-based infusion device must aim for. Ausems carried out this research as his doctoral work at the University of Leiden.

Ausems collaborated with Carl C. Hug Jr., Donald R. Stanski, and Anton G. L. Burm — a partnership spanning the Leiden and U.S. (Emory/Stanford) pharmacology groups — and subsequently compared computer-assisted (target-controlled) infusion against intermittent bolus administration of alfentanil, helping to demonstrate that model-driven infusion produces more stable and predictable opioid concentrations.

*Key reference:* Ausems ME, Hug CC Jr, Stanski DR, Burm AGL. Plasma concentrations of alfentanil required to supplement nitrous oxide anesthesia for general surgery. Anesthesiology. 1986;65(4):362–373.

---

**James G. Bovill** — anesthesiologist; Professor of Anaesthesia, Leiden University Medical Center; opioid PK/PD in cardiac anesthesia

Bovill, trained in Belfast, was a leading figure in intravenous and cardiac anesthesia and a driving force behind the Leiden opioid PK/PD program. His early work at the University of Amsterdam, where he was senior lecturer from 1977 to 1985, established the pharmacokinetics of high-dose fentanyl in patients undergoing cardiac surgery, including the effect of cardiopulmonary bypass on plasma concentrations, and he extended this to comparative studies of fentanyl, sufentanil, and alfentanil in cardiac and valvular surgery. With Peter Sebel and others he correlated opioid dosing with electroencephalographic (EEG) measures of drug effect, an important step toward quantitative opioid pharmacodynamics.

At Leiden, where he was Professor of Anaesthesia from 1985 to 2007, Bovill fostered the intravenous-anesthesia group whose propofol–opioid interaction and TCI research (Vuyk, Engbers, Burm) became internationally influential; he is a co-author on the landmark Vuyk interaction studies. His opioid PK/PD work fed directly into the effect-compartment and TCI modeling that underlies systems developed in the broader community.

*Key references:* Bovill JG, Sebel PS. Pharmacokinetics of high-dose fentanyl: a study in patients undergoing cardiac surgery. Br J Anaesth. 1980;52(8):795–801. • Bovill JG, Sebel PS, Stanley TH. Opioid analgesics in anesthesia: with special reference to their use in cardiovascular anesthesia. Anesthesiology. 1984;61(6):731–755.

---

**Anton G. L. Burm** — clinical pharmacologist, Department of Anaesthesiology, Leiden University Medical Center (LUMC)

Burm was the clinical-pharmacology anchor of the Leiden intravenous-anesthesia group, specializing in the pharmacokinetics of local anesthetics and opioids. He pioneered the use of stable-isotope (deuterium-labelled) methods to separate systemic absorption from disposition after epidural and subarachnoid administration: by giving a labelled analogue intravenously at the moment of neuraxial dosing, he could resolve the two processes from a single set of plasma samples — work he later extended to the effect of age on bupivacaine absorption and disposition. He also characterized the stereoselective (enantiomer-specific) pharmacokinetics of bupivacaine, showing that after intravenous administration of the racemate the R(+)- and S(−)-enantiomers differ in clearance, volume of distribution, and plasma protein binding — pharmacokinetic background to the later clinical adoption of the single-enantiomer local anesthetic levobupivacaine.

Within the Leiden group, Burm was a recurring co-author on the propofol–opioid interaction and TCI studies led by Vuyk and Bovill, contributing pharmacokinetic modeling and assay expertise. His methods connect to the wider PK/PD community that produced the target-controlled infusion models used in tools such as STANPUMP.

*Key references:* Burm AGL, Vermeulen NPE, van Kleef JW, de Boer AG, Spierdijk J, Breimer DD. Pharmacokinetics of lignocaine and bupivacaine in surgical patients following epidural administration: simultaneous investigation of absorption and disposition kinetics using stable isotopes. Clin Pharmacokinet. 1987;13(3):191–203. • Burm AG, van der Meer AD, van Kleef JW, Zeijlmans PW, Groen K. Pharmacokinetics of the enantiomers of bupivacaine following intravenous administration of the racemate. Br J Clin Pharmacol. 1994;38(2):125–129.

---

**Albert Dahan** — professor of anesthesiology, Leiden University Medical Center; quantitative pharmacology of opioid-induced respiratory depression

Dahan has been professor of anesthesiology at Leiden University Medical Center since 2004, where he founded and long led the institution's anesthesia and pain research unit. His central contribution is the quantitative pharmacology of opioid-induced respiratory depression: rather than treating apnea as a binary adverse event, his group measured the ventilatory response to hypercapnia and hypoxia as a continuous, graded pharmacodynamic endpoint and fitted explicit pharmacokinetic–pharmacodynamic models to it. His 2010 review with Leon Aarts and T. W. Smith on the incidence, reversal, and prevention of opioid-induced respiratory depression remains among the most widely cited syntheses of that literature.

Much of the modeling was done with the Leiden pharmacometrician Erik Olofsen, a collaboration spanning well over a hundred joint publications. With Yassen, Olofsen, and Meindert Danhof, Dahan built mechanism-based models that separate blood–effect-site equilibration from receptor association–dissociation kinetics, showing that the hysteresis between fentanyl concentration and respiratory depression is explained by biophase distribution alone (equilibration half-life about 16 min), whereas buprenorphine's far slower profile (about 75 min) additionally reflects slow mu-opioid receptor association and dissociation kinetics. The same analysis separately estimated buprenorphine's intrinsic activity at 0.56 against fentanyl's 0.91 — the partial agonism that produces buprenorphine's ceiling effect on ventilation. Related work with Olofsen and Sarton modeled naloxone reversal of morphine- and morphine-6-glucuronide-induced respiratory depression, and population PK/PD analyses with Sigtermans characterized the analgesic and cardiovascular effects of S(+)-ketamine.

Dahan worked alongside the Leiden intravenous-anesthesia group of Jaap Vuyk, Frank Engbers, and Anton Burm. With Engbers he wrote a pointed assessment of target-controlled infusion after two decades of clinical use, cataloguing the anomalies that arise when open TCI systems offer competing pharmacokinetic models for the same drug, when anthropometric covariate relationships are extrapolated beyond the populations from which they were derived, and when regulatory requirements for drug–model pairings remain unsettled — cautions that apply directly to anyone selecting a model for simulation or infusion control.

*Key references:* Dahan A, Aarts L, Smith TW. Incidence, reversal, and prevention of opioid-induced respiratory depression. Anesthesiology. 2010;112(1):226–238. • Engbers FHM, Dahan A. Anomalies in target-controlled infusion: an analysis after 20 years of clinical use. Anaesthesia. 2018;73(5):619–630.

---

**Meindert Danhof** — professor emeritus of pharmacology, Leiden Academic Centre for Drug Research

Danhof built his career at Leiden University, where he took his doctorate under Douwe Breimer in 1980, held the chair of pharmacology in both the Faculty of Science and the Faculty of Medicine, and served as scientific director of the Leiden Academic Centre for Drug Research (LACDR) from 2005 to 2013 before retiring in 2017. Between the doctorate and the chair he spent three years as a postdoctoral fellow with Gerhard Levy at the State University of New York at Buffalo. He is the principal architect of *mechanism-based* pharmacokinetic–pharmacodynamic modeling: the program of replacing empirical concentration–effect curves with models whose terms correspond to identifiable biological steps — distribution to the biophase, target binding and activation, transduction, and homeostatic feedback. Its central methodological claim, set out in his 2007 review, is that such models separate *drug-specific* parameters (receptor affinity, intrinsic efficacy) from *system-specific* parameters (receptor density, transduction capacity, homeostatic set points). That separation is what allows a pharmacodynamic model to be carried across drugs acting on the same system, and across species and patient populations for the same drug.

The experimental foundation of this work was the use of the EEG as a continuous, graded measure of central drug effect, which supplies the dense effect-versus-time data that hysteresis-based estimation of effect-site equilibration requires. Danhof's group applied it systematically to benzodiazepines and to opioids, relating EEG response to concentration through effect-compartment and receptor-binding models and estimating biophase equilibration rates. The approach connects directly to anesthesia: with Donald Stanski and William Ebling he characterized the EEG pharmacodynamics of thiopental in the rat, and with Cornelis Bol, Stanski, and Jaap Mandema the hypnotic, EEG, cardiovascular, and ventilatory responses to dexmedetomidine in the same preparation. He was the senior author on the Leiden studies of Mandema — also listed in this panel — including the midazolam and alpha-hydroxymidazolam work that separated the contributions of a parent drug and its active metabolite to a single measured CNS effect.

Danhof's later work extended these ideas toward systems pharmacology and physiology-based pharmacodynamics, and in 2007 he founded the TI Pharma mechanism-based PK/PD modeling platform to assemble a shared model library for drug discovery and development. He received the Høst Madsen Medal, the highest scientific award of the International Pharmaceutical Federation, in 2019.

*Key references:* Mandema JW, Tuk B, van Steveninck AL, Breimer DD, Cohen AF, Danhof M. Pharmacokinetic-pharmacodynamic modeling of the central nervous system effects of midazolam and its main metabolite alpha-hydroxymidazolam in healthy volunteers. Clin Pharmacol Ther. 1992;51(6):715–728. • Danhof M, de Jongh J, De Lange EC, Della Pasqua O, Ploeger BA, Voskuyl RA. Mechanism-based pharmacokinetic-pharmacodynamic modeling: biophase distribution, receptor theory, and dynamical systems analysis. Annu Rev Pharmacol Toxicol. 2007;47:357–400.

**Frank H. M. Engbers** — anesthesiologist (now retired), Leiden University Medical Center; clinical implementation of target-controlled infusion

Engbers is a clinician-implementer of target-controlled infusion, focused on making TCI and effect-site targeting practical, safe, and teachable at the bedside. He co-authored the Leiden propofol–alfentanil interaction studies (providing the TCI delivery), and he became a widely cited authority on the clinical behavior of TCI systems — the proliferation of pharmacokinetic models in open TCI pumps, the pitfalls of extrapolating anthropometric data, effect-site ("effect-compartment") steering, and the regulatory ambiguities of TCI practice. His analyses of TCI "anomalies" after two decades of clinical use are standard reading for understanding why different pumps and models can produce different infusions for the same target.

Engbers has also been central to TCI education and simulation: he wrote TIVA Trainer, the teaching program that lets clinicians visualize predicted plasma and effect-site concentrations for a wide range of drugs and models. His clinical-implementation perspective links the Leiden group to the broader TCI community and to the ongoing standardization of TCI models.

*Key reference:* Engbers FHM, Dahan A. Anomalies in target-controlled infusion: an analysis after 20 years of clinical use. Anaesthesia. 2018;73(5):619–630.

**Erik Olofsen** — mathematical modeler, Department of Anesthesiology, Leiden University Medical Center

Erik Olofsen is the quantitative analyst behind much of the pharmacokinetic–pharmacodynamic output of the Leiden anesthesiology group. A mathematical modeler rather than a clinician, he has been the modeling half of a decades-long partnership with Albert Dahan, and he supplied the analysis for the earlier Leiden studies led by Jaap Vuyk with Anton Burm and James Bovill. He is a co-author of the 1997 study that defined the optimal EC50–EC95 propofol–opioid concentration pairs assuring adequate anesthesia with a rapid return of consciousness, and of the later mixed-effects analysis with Martijn Mertens showing that alfentanil alters propofol pharmacokinetics — evidence that anesthetic interaction is pharmacokinetic as well as pharmacodynamic.

With Dahan he characterized the dynamic relationship between end-tidal sevoflurane and isoflurane concentrations and two EEG-derived measures of drug effect, the bispectral index and the 95% spectral edge frequency. Fitting an effect-compartment model, they estimated effect-site equilibration half-lives (t½ke0) of a few minutes for both agents — the precise value depending on which EEG measure is used — and found isoflurane the more potent of the two. The paper remains a standard reference for applying the ke0 formalism to volatile anesthetics and for the hysteresis-collapse approach to EEG measures of anesthetic depth.

Olofsen's largest body of work concerns opioid-induced respiratory depression and the control of breathing, where he has built the PK/PD models underpinning Leiden's experimental studies — including population analyses of tolerance to respiratory depression in chronic high-dose opioid users. Ketamine and esketamine PK/PD form a second sustained theme, much of it with Marieke Niesters and Monique van Velzen. He also writes on methodology itself, including a widely used review with Dahan on population pharmacokinetic/pharmacodynamic modeling of anesthetics.

*Key references:* Vuyk J, Mertens MJ, Olofsen E, Burm AG, Bovill JG. Propofol anesthesia and rational opioid selection: determination of optimal EC50–EC95 propofol-opioid concentrations that assure adequate anesthesia and a rapid return of consciousness. Anesthesiology. 1997;87(6):1549–1562. • Olofsen E, Dahan A. The dynamic relationship between end-tidal sevoflurane and isoflurane concentrations and bispectral index and spectral edge frequency of the electroencephalogram. Anesthesiology. 1999;90(5):1345–1353.

**Jaap Vuyk** — anesthesiologist, Leiden University Medical Center; propofol–opioid interaction and response-surface modeling

Vuyk is best known for defining the pharmacodynamic interaction between propofol and opioids and translating it into rational dosing. Using computer-controlled (target-controlled) infusion of both drugs, his Leiden studies quantified how propofol reduces alfentanil requirements and how alfentanil lowers the propofol concentration at which patients wake, mapping the synergy across clinical endpoints. He then used concentration-pair (iso-effect) modeling to identify the optimal EC50–EC95 propofol–opioid concentration combinations that provide adequate anesthesia while assuring the most rapid return of consciousness, and later applied formal response-surface methods to the propofol–remifentanil interaction with Mertens — the conceptual basis for interaction-guided TCI dosing and a direct antecedent of the interaction facets used in modern PK/PD tools.

This work was performed with the Leiden group (Engbers, Burm, Bovill, Olofsen, Mertens) and connects closely to the wider TCI and interaction-modeling community (Shafer/STANPUMP; Minto and Schnider's response-surface methods; Struys' closed-loop and TCI research). Vuyk's optimal-concentration framework remains a standard reference for combining hypnotics and opioids.

*Key references:* Vuyk J, Lim T, Engbers FH, Burm AG, Vletter AA, Bovill JG. The pharmacodynamic interaction of propofol and alfentanil during lower abdominal surgery in women. Anesthesiology. 1995;83(1):8–22. • Vuyk J, Mertens MJ, Olofsen E, Burm AG, Bovill JG. Propofol anesthesia and rational opioid selection: determination of optimal EC50–EC95 propofol–opioid concentrations that assure adequate anesthesia and a rapid return of consciousness. Anesthesiology. 1997;87(6):1549–1562.

## Northwestern University

**Michael J. Avram** — pharmacologist/analytical chemist; recirculatory pharmacokinetic modeling and precise marker kinetics (Feinberg School of Medicine)

Michael Avram is Associate Professor Emeritus of Anesthesiology at Northwestern University's Feinberg School of Medicine, a pharmacologist whose analytical rigor and quantitative modeling anchored the department's recirculatory pharmacokinetics program. His high-precision assay methods — resolving indocyanine green, thiopental, antipyrine, and other markers and drugs in arterial samples drawn at few-second intervals — made it possible to characterize the earliest, fastest phase of drug disposition after intravenous injection. With his long-standing collaborator Tom Krejcie (and Thomas Henthorn), Avram built recirculatory models that decompose early kinetics into circulatory mixing, first-pass pulmonary uptake, and rapid peripheral distribution, using co-administered markers of blood, extracellular fluid, and total body water.

This body of work reframed how the onset of rapidly acting anesthetics is understood: front-end kinetics, driven by cardiac output and mixing, determine the arterial and effect-site concentration profile in the critical first minutes, informing bolus dosing strategy and the physiologic basis of plasma-to-effect-site equilibration used in TCI.

*Key references:* Avram MJ, Krejcie TC, Henthorn TK. The relationship of age to the pharmacokinetics of early drug distribution: the concurrent disposition of thiopental and indocyanine green. Anesthesiology. 1990;72(3):403–411. • Krejcie TC, Avram MJ. What determines anesthetic induction dose? It's the front-end kinetics, doctor! Anesth Analg. 1999;89(3):541–544.

---

**Thomas K. Henthorn** — anesthesiologist and clinical pharmacologist; recirculatory/physiologic PK and front-end kinetics (Northwestern University; later Chair of Anesthesiology, University of Colorado, 2000–2016, where he remains Professor of Anesthesiology)

Thomas Henthorn trained at Northwestern University, where he was part of the recirculatory-modeling collaboration with Tom Krejcie and Michael Avram, and he later moved to the University of Colorado, where he is Professor of Anesthesiology (and Adjoint Professor of Pharmaceutical Sciences). His research centers on the pharmacokinetics of early drug distribution, physiologically based and recirculatory modeling, and the disposition of markers such as indocyanine green, with continued interests in drug transporters, metabolism, and pharmacogenetics.

Within the Northwestern program, Henthorn contributed to models that resolve the first-pass and rapid-distribution phase governing the onset of intravenous anesthetics and opioids. This front-end kinetic work clarifies how circulatory mixing and pulmonary uptake shape the arterial concentration profile immediately after injection — the phase most relevant to bolus dosing and to effect-site targeting in modern anesthetic delivery.

*Key references:* Avram MJ, Krejcie TC, Henthorn TK. The relationship of age to the pharmacokinetics of early drug distribution: the concurrent disposition of thiopental and indocyanine green. Anesthesiology. 1990;72(3):403–411. • Krejcie TC, Henthorn TK, Shanks CA, Avram MJ. A recirculatory pharmacokinetic model describing the circulatory mixing, tissue distribution and elimination of antipyrine in dogs. J Pharmacol Exp Ther. 1994;269(2):609–616.

---

**Tom C. Krejcie** — anesthesiologist; recirculatory ("front-end") pharmacokinetic modeling of early drug distribution (Feinberg School of Medicine)

Tom Krejcie is an anesthesiologist (now Professor Emeritus of Anesthesiology) at Northwestern University whose research, in close and long-standing collaboration with pharmacologist Michael J. Avram and anesthesiologist Thomas K. Henthorn, developed the recirculatory (front-end) approach to the pharmacokinetics of intravenously administered anesthetic drugs. Where classical compartmental models begin describing a drug only after blood-sampling "mixing," Krejcie and colleagues sampled arterial blood every few seconds after injection to characterize the first minutes of disposition — the circulatory mixing, first-pass pulmonary uptake, and rapid tissue distribution that determine the onset of rapidly acting IV drugs. Their models used simultaneously administered markers of intravascular space (indocyanine green), extracellular fluid, and total body water, together with anesthetic and analgesic drugs such as thiopental and fentanyl, to partition early kinetics into physiologically interpretable elements.

This front-end perspective is directly relevant to bolus and infusion behavior of anesthetics: it explains why peak effect-site concentration and time-to-peak depend on cardiac output and mixing, informing rational bolus dosing and the plasma–effect-site (ke0) relationships used in TCI.

*Key reference:* Krejcie TC, Henthorn TK, Shanks CA, Avram MJ. A recirculatory pharmacokinetic model describing the circulatory mixing, tissue distribution and elimination of antipyrine in dogs. J Pharmacol Exp Ther. 1994;269(2):609–616.

## Stanford University

**Corina Andresen** — research collaborator, Stanford University (Shafer laboratory)

Corina Andresen was a collaborator associated with Steven L. Shafer's Stanford group whose name appears as a co-author on several of the group's core intravenous-anesthetic modeling studies. She is credited on the Schnider propofol pharmacokinetic study that underlies the widely used propofol target-controlled infusion model, and on the Bouillon et al. remifentanil ventilatory-depression and propofol–remifentanil interaction papers. Her contribution to this body of work is as a co-investigator and co-author on those studies rather than as an independent author of the anesthesia PK/PD literature.

*Key references:* Schnider TW, Minto CF, Gambus PL, Andresen C, Goodale DB, Shafer SL, Youngs EJ. The influence of method of administration and covariates on the pharmacokinetics of propofol in adult volunteers. Anesthesiology. 1998;88(5):1170–1182. • Bouillon T, Bruhn J, Radu-Radulescu L, Andresen C, Cohane C, Shafer SL. A model of the ventilatory depressant potency of remifentanil in the non–steady state. Anesthesiology. 2003;99(4):779–787. • Bouillon TW, Bruhn J, Radulescu L, Andresen C, Shafer TJ, Cohane C, Shafer SL. Pharmacodynamic interaction between propofol and remifentanil regarding hypnosis, tolerance of laryngoscopy, bispectral index, and electroencephalographic approximate entropy. Anesthesiology. 2004;100(6):1353–1372.

**Martin S. Angst** — anesthesiologist and clinical pharmacologist, Stanford University; opioid-induced hyperalgesia and human experimental-pain pharmacodynamics

Martin S. Angst is Professor of Anesthesiology, Perioperative and Pain Medicine at Stanford University, where he also serves as Vice Chair for Strategy and Initiatives. His research program is built on human experimental-pain models — quantitative sensory testing in healthy volunteers combined with controlled intravenous opioid administration — used to characterize opioid pharmacodynamics with the same rigor usually reserved for pharmacokinetics. With J. David Clark he wrote the qualitative systematic review that consolidated the evidence for opioid-induced hyperalgesia and made the phenomenon a mainstream clinical concern in anesthesiology and pain medicine.

His experimental work established that hyperalgesia can emerge rapidly after opioid exposure: with Wolfgang Koppert, Martin Schmelz, and Clark, he showed that a short remifentanil infusion in humans produces an expansion of mechanical hyperalgesia around an experimentally sensitized skin area during the withdrawal period, an effect abolished by co-administration of the NMDA-receptor antagonist S-ketamine, which the authors took as evidence for a role of the NMDA-receptor system. He pursued the relationship to tolerance directly with Steven L. Shafer, J. David Clark, and David R. Drover in a placebo-controlled study of a three-hour remifentanil infusion, which found no detectable acute tolerance to analgesic, respiratory-depressant, or sedative opioid effects — an important negative result for how acute opioid effect is modeled. With Laura C. Lazzeroni, Gary E. Swan, and colleagues he then applied a monozygotic/dizygotic twin paradigm to quantify the heritability of pain sensitivity, opioid analgesia, and the aversive and reinforcing effects of opioids.

Earlier in his career Angst worked within the Stanford pharmacokinetic–pharmacodynamic group led by Donald R. Stanski, contributing to studies of opioid disposition and effect in which David R. Drover and Davide Verotta carried out population pharmacokinetic analysis in NONMEM alongside concentration–effect measurement, including work on immediate- and extended-release oral hydromorphone. More recently his focus has shifted to perioperative recovery and resilience, using surgery as a controlled injury model; with Brice Gaudillière and Garry P. Nolan he co-authored the single-cell mass cytometry study showing that immune signatures measured shortly after surgery correlate with the subsequent clinical recovery trajectory.

*Key references:* Angst MS, Koppert W, Pahl I, Clark DJ, Schmelz M. Short-term infusion of the mu-opioid agonist remifentanil in humans causes hyperalgesia during withdrawal. Pain. 2003;106(1–2):49–57. • Angst MS, Clark JD. Opioid-induced hyperalgesia: a qualitative systematic review. Anesthesiology. 2006;104(3):570–587.

**Jessica R. Ansari** — obstetric anesthesiologist, Stanford University; pharmacokinetics of intravenous calcium in pregnancy and the pharmacology of uterine tone

Jessica R. Ansari is Assistant Professor of Anesthesiology, Perioperative and Pain Medicine (Obstetrics) at Stanford University School of Medicine, where she practices obstetric anesthesia. Her research treats a familiar rescue drug as an open pharmacokinetic question: calcium is given routinely for uterine atony and postpartum hemorrhage, yet the dose, the salt, and the time course of the resulting change in ionized calcium had been little studied in pregnant patients. Working within the Stanford obstetric anesthesia group with Brendan Carvalho and colleagues, she has built a body of work running from bedside pharmacokinetics through randomized trials to the receptor-level mechanism.

The pharmacokinetic core of that work is a bioequivalence (dose-ratio) trial of intravenous calcium during cesarean delivery, conducted with Steven L. Shafer. It addressed two questions clinical practice had largely assumed answers to: how calcium gluconate and calcium chloride compare on a milligram basis, and how quickly an administered dose dissipates. Across 34 participants the two salts proved equipotent at a 3:1 gluconate-to-chloride dose ratio, and a population pharmacokinetic analysis drawn from 70 patients found that a 1-gram infusion of calcium chloride raised ionized calcium by about 0.39 mM at peak, with that increase halving roughly 29 minutes after the start of the 10-minute infusion — a brief enough exposure to constrain how calcium can plausibly be timed against uterine contraction. This followed her earlier pilot randomized trial and pharmacokinetic study in 40 cesarean patients with atony risk factors, in which a 1-gram calcium chloride infusion was well tolerated and raised ionized calcium from a baseline near 1.18 mmol/L to a peak of roughly 1.50–1.60 mmol/L. In a subsequent single-center randomized trial of 120 laboring patients requiring intrapartum cesarean delivery, calcium did not significantly reduce median blood loss in the primary analysis, though a planned subgroup analysis showed a reduction.

Alongside the clinical pharmacology she has pursued the mechanism by which calcium and oxytocin interact in myometrium, studying the intracellular calcium response to oxytocin in uterine smooth muscle cells from patients with clinically diagnosed uterine atony, and co-authoring work identifying transient receptor potential vanilloid 4 (TRPV4) channel activation as a route by which oxytocin induces contraction in gravid human uterine smooth muscle. Her broader obstetric pharmacology includes the review of the pharmacokinetics and pharmacodynamics of drugs commonly used in pregnancy and parturition, written with Brendan Carvalho, Steven L. Shafer, and Pamela Flood, and a matched cohort study with Flood and Shafer reporting an association between unintentional dural puncture during epidural anesthesia and chronic disabling postpartum headache; she was a member of the multisociety international working group that produced the 2023 consensus practice guidelines on postdural puncture headache.

*Key references:* Ansari JR, Kalariya N, Carvalho B, Flood P, Guo N, Riley E. Calcium chloride for the prevention of uterine atony during cesarean delivery: a pilot randomized controlled trial and pharmacokinetic study. J Clin Anesth. 2022;80:110796. • Ansari JR, Conti DJ, Michel G, Yarmosh A, Cole NM, Shafer SL. Bioequivalence and pharmacokinetics of intravenous calcium during cesarean delivery. Anesthesiology. 2025;142(1):121–131.
