**Juliana Barr** — anesthesiologist and intensivist; research fellow with Steven L. Shafer at Stanford; PK/PD-based sedation in the intensive care unit

Juliana Barr is Professor of Anesthesiology, Perioperative and Pain Medicine, Emerita, at Stanford University School of Medicine, and has served as a staff anesthesiologist and intensivist at the VA Palo Alto Health Care System since 1992. She is board certified in internal medicine, anesthesiology, and critical care medicine, and completed a postdoctoral research fellowship in clinical pharmacology at Stanford before joining the faculty. At the Palo Alto VA she co-founded the first intensivist-led ICU team in 1993 and later established a VA ICU nurse practitioner program.

Barr's laboratory work applied integrated pharmacokinetic–pharmacodynamic modeling to sedative dosing in critically ill adults — the same modeling approach that underlies this program. With Talmage D. Egan, Katie Zomorodi, Pedro L. Gambús and Steven L. Shafer she characterized propofol pharmacokinetics and pharmacodynamics in ICU patients and converted the combined model into practical infusion regimens targeting defined levels of sedation. In a companion trial published in the same issue of *Anesthesiology*, she compared intravenous lorazepam with midazolam for ICU sedation using a pharmacologic model. She was also a co-author of the midazolam target-controlled infusion study in patients recovering from coronary artery bypass grafting, contributing to the population pharmacokinetic analysis; the paired pharmacodynamic analysis of that dataset was reported by Jacques Somma and colleagues.

Barr subsequently led the Society of Critical Care Medicine's clinical practice guidelines for the management of pain, agitation and delirium (PAD) in adult ICU patients, serving as first author of the 2013 guidelines, which reshaped sedation and analgesia practice by favoring analgesia-first, lighter and more carefully titrated sedation with routine delirium monitoring. She is a founding member of the society's ICU Liberation Campaign and contributed to the development of the ABCDEF bundle.

*Key references:* Barr J, Egan TD, Sandoval NF, Zomorodi K, Cohane C, Gambus PL, et al. Propofol dosing regimens for ICU sedation based upon an integrated pharmacokinetic-pharmacodynamic model. Anesthesiology. 2001;95(2):324–333. • Barr J, Fraser GL, Puntillo K, Ely EW, Gélinas C, Dasta JF, et al. Clinical practice guidelines for the management of pain, agitation, and delirium in adult patients in the intensive care unit. Crit Care Med. 2013;41(1):263–306.

---

**Valérie Billard** — anesthesiologist; research fellow with Steven L. Shafer at Stanford (later Institut Gustave Roussy, Villejuif, France)

Valérie Billard is a French anesthesiologist whose foundational pharmacodynamic work was done as a research fellow in Steven L. Shafer's laboratory at Stanford, in close collaboration with Donald R. Stanski's group. There she investigated quantitative electroencephalographic (EEG) measures of anesthetic drug effect, comparing processed-EEG descriptors as pharmacodynamic endpoints for intravenous anesthetics and opioids. Her best-known study, co-authored with Pedro L. Gambús, systematically compared spectral edge frequency, delta power, and the bispectral index (BIS) as measures of the drug effect of alfentanil, propofol, and midazolam, characterizing the concentration–effect relationship and the temporal (ke0) delay between plasma concentration and EEG effect for each agent. This work helped establish BIS and related EEG measures as pharmacodynamic tools for the intravenous hypnotics — bispectral index, spectral edge, and delta power yielded similar IC50 and ke0 estimates, although BIS modeled alfentanil effect less well than the other descriptors — and it informed subsequent modeling of hypnotic–opioid interaction.

After her Stanford fellowship, Billard returned to France, where she has been an anesthesiologist at the Institut Gustave Roussy in Villejuif, with continuing interests in anesthetic drug pharmacology, drug delivery and target-controlled infusion (TCI), and intraoperative monitoring.

*Key reference:* Billard V, Gambus PL, Chamoun N, Stanski DR, Shafer SL. A comparison of spectral edge, delta power, and bispectral index as EEG measures of alfentanil, propofol, and midazolam drug effect. Clin Pharmacol Ther. 1997;61(1):45–58.

---

**Thomas W. Bouillon** — anesthesiologist and clinical pharmacologist; research fellow with Steven L. Shafer at Stanford, 1997–1999 (later University of Bern and the pharmaceutical industry); response-surface modeling of the propofol–remifentanil interaction

Thomas Bouillon is an anesthesiologist and clinical pharmacologist whose work centers on the quantitative PK/PD of intravenous anesthetics. As a research fellow in Steven L. Shafer's laboratory at Stanford, he became a leading contributor to response-surface modeling of the propofol–remifentanil interaction, characterizing how a hypnotic and an opioid combine across the full range of clinically relevant effect-site concentrations rather than at isolated dose pairs. His landmark 2004 study quantified the interaction for multiple endpoints simultaneously — hypnosis (no response to shaking and shouting), tolerance of laryngoscopy, and the processed-EEG measures bispectral index (BIS) and approximate entropy — demonstrating marked synergy for the clinical endpoints while the EEG measures behaved more additively. This work is a cornerstone of modern effect-site-targeted, interaction-aware anesthetic dosing.

Bouillon also made foundational contributions to modeling opioid-induced ventilatory depression, applying indirect-effect (non–steady-state) models to arterial and end-tidal CO2 during and after remifentanil administration — quantifying the potency and time course of respiratory depression and underscoring the hazard of bolus dosing of fast-onset opioids in spontaneously breathing patients. After his Stanford fellowship he worked in Switzerland at the Department of Anaesthesiology, Inselspital, University of Bern (with Martin Luginbühl's group), and subsequently moved into the pharmaceutical industry as a pharmacometrician (including at Novartis, Basel).

*Key references:* Bouillon T, Bruhn J, Radu-Radulescu L, Andresen C, Cohane C, Shafer SL. A model of the ventilatory depressant potency of remifentanil in the non–steady state. Anesthesiology. 2003;99(4):779–787. • Bouillon TW, Bruhn J, Radulescu L, Andresen C, Shafer TJ, Cohane C, Shafer SL. Pharmacodynamic interaction between propofol and remifentanil regarding hypnosis, tolerance of laryngoscopy, bispectral index, and electroencephalographic approximate entropy. Anesthesiology. 2004;100(6):1353–1372.

---

**Michael Bührer** — clinical pharmacologist; quantitative EEG pharmacodynamics of benzodiazepines, Stanford University

Michael Bührer worked in Donald Stanski's anesthesia clinical-pharmacology group at Stanford, together with Pierre Maitre, on the quantitative electroencephalographic pharmacodynamics of benzodiazepines. In a paired series of studies he first addressed the measurement problem — selecting an EEG parameter that reliably and monotonically tracks benzodiazepine (midazolam) drug effect on the central nervous system — and then applied that parameter to build parametric and nonparametric PK/PD models comparing midazolam and diazepam.

Using arterial plasma concentrations linked to EEG effect through an effect-compartment (ke0) model, Bührer and colleagues quantified each drug's intrinsic steady-state potency and the half-time of blood–brain equilibration, finding midazolam roughly five-fold more potent than diazepam and with slower CNS equilibration (about 4.8 vs. 1.6 minutes). This careful separation of pharmacokinetics from pharmacodynamics via the effect site, using the EEG as the effect measure, is a foundational example of the effect-site/EEG PD framework that underpins TCI and stanpumpR's effect-site simulation.

*Key reference:* Bührer M, Maitre PO, Crevoisier C, Stanski DR. Electroencephalographic effects of benzodiazepines. II. Pharmacodynamic modeling of the electroencephalographic effects of midazolam and diazepam. Clin Pharmacol Ther. 1990;48(5):555–567.

---

**David R. Drover** — anesthesiologist and clinical pharmacologist, Stanford University; population PK/PD of intravenous anesthetics and processed-EEG measures of drug effect

David R. Drover is Professor of Anesthesiology, Perioperative and Pain Medicine, Emeritus, at Stanford University School of Medicine. He trained in medicine and anesthesia at Dalhousie University and then came to Stanford, where he has spent his academic career. His research has centered on the pharmacokinetics and pharmacodynamics of intravenous anesthetics, opioids, and sedatives, with a recurring emphasis on population modeling of concentration–effect relationships in groups that are difficult to study, including neonates, infants, children, and obstetric patients.

With Harry J. M. Lemmens, Drover characterized the population pharmacokinetics and pharmacodynamics of remifentanil during nitrous oxide anesthesia for abdominal surgery. Stable blood concentrations were established with a computer-controlled infusion pump — the research forerunner of target-controlled infusion — and the concentration–response data were analyzed with NONMEM. The study described a two-compartment disposition model incorporating lean body mass as a size covariate, and estimated the blood concentration associated with a 50% probability of adequate anesthesia (Cb50) as 4.1 ng/mL in men and 7.5 ng/mL in women, a difference the authors cautioned might reflect the mix of surgical procedures rather than an intrinsic pharmacodynamic sex effect.

Drover has also worked extensively on processed-EEG measures of drug effect. He led the multicenter randomized trial showing that titrating propofol to the Patient State Index — a quantitative EEG-derived index of hypnotic state — shortened emergence and recovery and modestly reduced propofol delivery without increasing unwanted events or reported awareness, and he has since contributed to comparative evaluations of the Patient State Index, Bispectral Index, and entropy monitors. In pediatric and volunteer clinical pharmacology he has collaborated with Gregory B. Hammer and with Steven L. Shafer, including work on the propofol EC50 during endoscopy in children and on the pharmacodynamic interaction of propofol and remifentanil in children, and with Martin S. Angst and Shafer on the analgesic, sedative, and respiratory pharmacodynamics of opioids in human volunteers.

*Key references:* Drover DR, Lemmens HJ. Population pharmacodynamics and pharmacokinetics of remifentanil as a supplement to nitrous oxide anesthesia for elective abdominal surgery. Anesthesiology. 1998;89(4):869–877. • Drover DR, Lemmens HJ, Pierce ET, et al. Patient State Index: titration of delivery and recovery from propofol, alfentanil, and nitrous oxide anesthesia. Anesthesiology. 2002;97(1):82–89.

---

**William F. "Bill" Ebling** — pharmacokineticist and pharmaceutical scientist; physiologically based and simulation modeling of intravenous anesthetics, Stanford University

Bill Ebling worked with Donald Stanski's group at Stanford on the pharmacokinetics and pharmacodynamics of intravenous anesthetics, including thiopental, fentanyl, and alfentanil. He was an early proponent of using computer simulation — rather than isolated parameter tables — to make integrated PK/PD behavior clinically interpretable, showing how the time course of plasma concentration, the estimated effect-site concentration, and the intensity of EEG-measured CNS effect combine to produce a drug's clinical profile. His comparative simulations of fentanyl and alfentanil demonstrated that differences in blood–brain (effect-site) equilibration rate, rather than plasma pharmacokinetics alone, explain the differing onset and offset of clinical effect between opioids.

Ebling also pursued physiologically based pharmacokinetic modeling of these agents, connecting tissue-level distribution to the whole-body disposition used in dosing simulation. This simulation-and-effect-site perspective — computing predicted effect-site concentrations from closed-form models and displaying the resulting time course — is the same conceptual engine at the heart of TCI and of stanpumpR's plasma- and effect-site concentration displays.

*Key reference:* Ebling WF, Lee EN, Stanski DR. Understanding pharmacokinetics and pharmacodynamics through computer stimulation [sic — the printed and PubMed-indexed title reads "stimulation"]: I. The comparative clinical profiles of fentanyl and alfentanil. Anesthesiology. 1990;72(4):650–658. (PMID 2321782)

---

**Pamela Flood** — anesthesiologist and clinical pharmacologist; Professor (retired), Stanford University; pharmacokinetics and pharmacodynamics of drugs in pregnancy

Pamela Flood was Professor in the Department of Anesthesiology, Perioperative and Pain Medicine at Stanford University until her retirement in 2023, and continues as an adjunct professor. She took her medical degree, internal medicine internship, anesthesiology residency, and an obstetric anesthesiology fellowship at Columbia University and New York-Presbyterian Hospital, and later completed a pain medicine fellowship at Stanford. Before moving to Stanford she was on the anesthesiology faculty at Columbia University — much of her obstetric work was based in that department's Obstetrical Division — and subsequently in the Department of Anesthesia and Perioperative Care at the University of California, San Francisco.

Her most directly pharmacokinetic contribution is a systematic account of how pregnancy changes drug disposition and dose requirement. With Jessica Ansari, Brendan Carvalho, and Steven L. Shafer she wrote a comprehensive review of the pharmacokinetics and pharmacodynamics of the drugs most commonly given during pregnancy and parturition, arguing that the physiological changes of pregnancy alter bioavailability, distribution, and clearance in ways that are not reliably predictable from non-pregnant data, and that many established dosing recommendations for pregnant patients had not been updated to reflect contemporary pharmacokinetic and pharmacodynamic measurements. This concern with quantitative dosing in the parturient runs through her broader obstetric anesthesia research, which has combined pharmacodynamic modeling with clinical trials and population-scale analyses: mathematical modeling of pain and cervical progress across the first stage of nulliparous labor (also with Shafer), studies of genetic sources of variability in labor pain and labor progress, and analyses of variation in the delivery of labor analgesia across hospitals.

A second, closely related line of her work concerns pain and analgesic requirement after childbirth. With Ryu Komatsu and Carvalho she characterized in detail the trajectory of pain, analgesic consumption, and functional recovery after nulliparous birth, and reviewed the factors associated with pain that persists after delivery. Related work has examined opioid prescribing and consumption after cesarean delivery. Separately, and earlier in her career, she established a mechanistic result still cited in the anesthetic mechanisms literature: that α4β2 neuronal nicotinic acetylcholine receptors are inhibited by isoflurane and propofol at clinically relevant concentrations while α7-type nicotinic receptors are not. She is also a co-author, with Steven L. Shafer, Jan F. A. Hendrickx, James M. Sonner, and Edmund I. "Ted" Eger II — Shafer, Hendrickx, and Eger all appear elsewhere in this panel — of the theoretical analysis of what additivity rather than synergy between inhaled anesthetics implies about their molecular sites of action.

*Key references:*

- Shafer SL, Hendrickx JF, Flood P, Sonner J, Eger EI 2nd. Additivity versus synergy: a theoretical analysis of implications for anesthetic mechanisms. Anesth Analg. 2008;107(2):507–524.
- Debiec J, Conell-Price J, Evansmith J, Shafer SL, Flood P. Mathematical modeling of the pain and progress of the first stage of nulliparous labor. Anesthesiology. 2009;111(5):1093–1110.
- Reitman E, Conell-Price J, Evansmith J, Olson L, Drosinos S, Jasper N, Randolph P, Smiley RM, Shafer S, Flood P. β2-adrenergic receptor genotype and other variables that contribute to labor pain and progress. Anesthesiology. 2011;114(4):927–939.
- Ansari J, Carvalho B, Shafer SL, Flood P. Pharmacokinetics and pharmacodynamics of drugs commonly used in pregnancy and parturition. Anesth Analg. 2016;122(3):786–804.

---

**Pedro L. Gambús** — anesthesiologist; research fellow in the Stanford/Palo Alto group; PK/PD modeling, EEG/BIS measures of drug effect, and anesthetic drug interactions (later Hospital Clínic de Barcelona)

Gambús specializes in the quantitative pharmacodynamics of anesthetic and analgesic drugs, using processed-EEG measures (including bispectral/EEG-derived endpoints) to characterize the time course of drug effect and to model the effect-site equilibration (ke0) that underlies effect-site targeting in TCI. His research addresses propofol and opioid pharmacodynamics and their synergistic interactions, an area central to how modern TCI systems combine hypnotic and opioid targets.

He is a co-author of the landmark Schnider propofol study, developed during his time in the Stanford/Palo Alto research group of Steven Shafer and Donald Stanski (with Thomas Schnider and Charles Minto) — the study that produced the pharmacokinetic parameters of the widely deployed "Schnider" propofol TCI model; the effect-site equilibration rate constant (ke0 = 0.456 min⁻¹) that completes that model came from the companion 1999 study of the influence of age on propofol pharmacodynamics, in which an EEG-derived measure of effect was used and on which Gambús is likewise a co-author. He subsequently led a PK/PD research program at the Hospital Clínic de Barcelona.

*Key references:* Schnider TW, Minto CF, Gambus PL, Andresen C, Goodale DB, Shafer SL, Youngs EJ. The influence of method of administration and covariates on the pharmacokinetics of propofol in adult volunteers. Anesthesiology. 1998;88(5):1170–1182. • Schnider TW, Minto CF, Shafer SL, Gambus PL, Andresen C, Goodale DB, Youngs EJ. The influence of age on propofol pharmacodynamics. Anesthesiology. 1999;90(6):1502–1516.

---

**Keith M. Gregg** — statistician, Department of Statistics, Stanford University; collaborator of the Stanford / Palo Alto VA anesthesia pharmacology group on effect-site TCI control algorithms

Keith M. Gregg collaborated with Steven L. Shafer at Stanford on the mathematics and control algorithms underpinning effect-site target-controlled infusion (TCI). With Shafer he co-authored the foundational paper describing how a computer-controlled infusion pump can be driven to reach and then hold a target concentration at the site of drug effect rather than in plasma. That work formalized the algorithms — built on the plasma–effect-site rate constant ke0 and the closed-form three-compartment model — for computing the sequence of infusion rates that produces the most rapid, non-overshooting approach to a specified effect-site target, and then maintains it. These algorithms became the effect-site targeting logic implemented in STANPUMP and, in turn, the conceptual basis for the effect-site (ke0) targeting that stanpumpR reproduces.

Gregg also contributed to the anesthetic drug-interaction literature as a co-author of the Minto response-surface model, which extended single-drug concentration–response relationships to a mathematically consistent surface describing hypnotic and opioid interactions (e.g., propofol with opioids) — the same class of response-surface interaction modeling reflected in stanpumpR's interaction facet.

*Key references:* Shafer SL, Gregg KM. Algorithms to rapidly achieve and maintain stable drug concentrations at the site of drug effect with a computer-controlled infusion pump. J Pharmacokinet Biopharm. 1992;20(2):147–169. • Minto CF, Schnider TW, Short TG, Gregg KM, Gentilini A, Shafer SL. Response surface model for anesthetic drug interactions. Anesthesiology. 2000;92(6):1603–1616.

---

**Jan F. A. Hendrickx** — anesthesiologist; research fellow with Steven L. Shafer at Stanford; inhaled-anesthetic uptake and kinetics (OLV Hospital, Aalst, Belgium)

Jan F. A. Hendrickx is a Belgian anesthesiologist based at the Department of Anesthesiology and Intensive Care of OLV Hospital in Aalst, Belgium. He holds academic appointments as Professor of Anesthesiology and Perioperative Medicine at Ghent University and as Professor in the Department of Anesthesiology at UZ Leuven and the Department of Cardiovascular Sciences at KU Leuven. He is an alumnus of the anesthesiology departments of Pittsburgh and of Stanford, where he worked with Steven L. Shafer on pharmacokinetic and pharmacodynamic modeling.

His principal research program is the quantitative side of inhaled anesthesia: the uptake, distribution and kinetics of volatile agents, and the low-flow and closed-circuit techniques that follow from them. This is the inhaled-agent counterpart to the intravenous kinetics stanpumpR simulates — the same accounting of dose, uptake and distribution, but with the anesthetic delivered through a breathing circuit rather than a vein. Working largely with Andre M. De Wolf, he has measured desflurane and isoflurane uptake during closed-circuit anesthesia, studied agent uptake during liver resection and transplantation, tested whether large-volume nitrous oxide uptake alone explains the second gas effect, compared agent consumption under automated closed-circuit versus low-flow delivery, and developed models that compute anesthetic agent consumption from inspired and end-expired concentrations, minute ventilation, fresh gas flow and dead space ventilation. More recent work applies the same consumption arithmetic to the greenhouse gas burden of volatile anesthetics across the fresh gas flow range.

Hendrickx also contributed directly to the anesthetic interaction literature represented elsewhere in this panel. With Edmund I. "Ted" Eger II, James M. Sonner and Steven L. Shafer — Eger and Shafer both appear as separate entries here — he reviewed whether anesthetic combinations producing hypnosis and immobility act synergistically or merely additively, reasoning that additivity implies a shared site of action while synergy implies distinct ones. That review appeared alongside a companion theoretical analysis by Shafer, Hendrickx, Pamela Flood, Sonner and Eger, and the pair together form a conceptual bridge to the response-surface interaction models of Minto, Short, Vuyk, Bouillon and Kern that underlie the propofol–opioid interaction display in this application.

*Key references:* Hendrickx JF, Soetens M, Van der Donck A, Meeuwis H, Smolders F, De Wolf AM. Uptake of desflurane and isoflurane during closed-circuit anesthesia with spontaneous and controlled mechanical ventilation. Anesth Analg. 1997;84(2):413–418. • Hendrickx JF, Eger EI 2nd, Sonner JM, Shafer SL. Is synergy the rule? A review of anesthetic interactions producing hypnosis and immobility. Anesth Analg. 2008;107(2):494–506.

---

**Chuanpu Hu** — pharmacometrician/statistician; PhD Stanford University; postdoctoral fellow, Stanford Department of Anesthesia (later industry pharmacometrics)

Chuanpu Hu earned his PhD at Stanford and worked with Steven L. Shafer's group in the Stanford Department of Anesthesia (postdoctoral fellowship in clinical pharmacology, mid-1990s) on the statistical and control-theoretic methodology of PK/PD modeling for anesthetic drugs. With Shafer and William S. Lovejoy he analyzed control strategies for the three-compartment PK/PD models that describe intravenous anesthetics, comparing a maximum a posteriori (MAP) Bayesian adaptive dosing strategy against a stochastic control strategy for holding a target drug effect when the individual patient's PK/PD parameters are uncertain — finding the Bayesian approach effective in general, but the stochastic strategy, which hedges against estimation error, better in high-risk situations — work directly relevant to the optimization and effect-site targeting logic used in target-controlled infusion.

Hu subsequently built a long career in pharmacometrics in the pharmaceutical industry, including senior scientific and directorial roles at Johnson & Johnson/Janssen and Bristol Myers Squibb (and, earlier, a period as a mathematical statistician at the FDA). His industry work centers on population PK/PD analysis, nonlinear mixed-effects modeling, exposure–response methodology, and simulation — the statistical toolkit that population anesthetic PK/PD models such as those in stanpumpR rely upon.

*Key reference:* Hu C, Lovejoy WS, Shafer SL. Comparison of some control strategies for three-compartment PK/PD models. J Pharmacokinet Biopharm. 1994;22(6):525–550.

---

**Orlando R. Hung** — anesthesiologist and clinical pharmacologist; research fellow with Steven L. Shafer at Stanford, 1988–1990 (later Dalhousie University, Halifax, Canada)

As a research fellow with Steven L. Shafer at Stanford from 1988 to 1990, working within the anesthesia clinical-pharmacology group of Donald R. Stanski and alongside John R. Varvel, Orlando R. Hung contributed to the quantitative characterization of intravenous anesthetic pharmacodynamics. His work centered on thiopental, using the quantitative electroencephalographic (EEG) measure the group had developed for that drug — the number of waves per second derived from aperiodic waveform analysis — to link measured drug effect to serum concentration, and then relating that EEG-based measure of drug effect to clinical signs of anesthetic depth. This line of research helped establish the effect-site concentration framework and the use of processed EEG as an objective, continuous measure of the central-nervous-system effect of intravenous anesthetics.

Hung is the lead author of the second paper in the Stanford thiopental pharmacodynamics series, which quantified the relationship between clinical depth of anesthesia (graded responses to escalating stimuli) and the concurrent EEG measure of thiopental effect. Together with the companion report defining the concentration–EEG relationship, this work is widely cited in the development of EEG-based depth-of-anesthesia monitoring and in models of intravenous anesthetic effect.

He subsequently built his career at Dalhousie University in Halifax, Nova Scotia, Canada, where he became widely known for research and device development in airway management.

*Key reference:* Hung OR, Varvel JR, Shafer SL, Stanski DR. Thiopental pharmacodynamics. II. Quantitation of clinical and electroencephalographic depth of anesthesia. Anesthesiology. 1992;77(2):237–244.

---

**Harry J. M. Lemmens** — anesthesiologist and clinical pharmacologist, Stanford University; opioid PK/PD and anesthetic dosing in obesity

Lemmens trained in the Netherlands, taking his medical degree at the University of Utrecht and completing his internship and residency at the University Hospital of Leiden. His early work there, with James Bovill, Anton Burm, and Pim Hennis, characterized the pharmacokinetics and pharmacodynamics of alfentanil, showing that alfentanil pharmacodynamics were essentially unchanged by age while its clearance declined with age in a gender-dependent manner — an early demonstration that age effects on kinetics and on drug sensitivity must be estimated separately before they can be used for dosing. He came to Stanford for an anesthesiology fellowship and remained on the faculty, where he is Professor of Anesthesiology, Perioperative and Pain Medicine. (Stanford records list his given name as Hendrikus; he publishes as Harry J. M. Lemmens.)

At Stanford he joined the opioid pharmacology group of Donald Stanski and Steven Shafer. He was a co-author, with Talmage Egan, Pierre Fiset, and colleagues, of the early volunteer pharmacokinetic study of remifentanil, and of the Minto and Schnider paper that developed the age- and lean-body-mass covariate model for remifentanil pharmacokinetics and pharmacodynamics — the model now implemented in most remifentanil target-controlled infusion devices and simulation programs. With Shafer and Stanski he applied EEG-based pharmacokinetic–pharmacodynamic modeling to the investigational opioid trefentanil, estimating its blood–effect-site equilibration half-time (the t½ke0 underlying effect-site simulation) as roughly 1.2 minutes against 0.6 minutes for alfentanil. He later worked with David Drover and co-investigators on the Patient State Index, an EEG-derived measure of anesthetic drug effect, and wrote a widely cited review of pharmacokinetic–pharmacodynamic relationships for opioids in balanced anesthesia.

Much of his subsequent work addresses anesthetic dosing in obesity and, specifically, which body-size descriptor a dose should be scaled to. With Jay Brodsky and Donald Bernstein he proposed estimating ideal body weight in kilograms as 22 × (height in metres)², a formula that falls midway among earlier published estimates and is now in common use. With Jerry Ingrande and Brodsky he showed that the induction dose of propofol in morbidly obese subjects scales with lean body weight rather than total body weight, a finding that underlies current recommendations for dose adjustment in the morbidly obese and for the body-weight descriptors used in dosing calculators and simulators.

*Key references:* Egan TD, Lemmens HJ, Fiset P, Hermann DJ, Muir KT, Stanski DR, et al. The pharmacokinetics of the new short-acting opioid remifentanil (GI87084B) in healthy adult male volunteers. Anesthesiology. 1993;79(5):881–892. • Ingrande J, Brodsky JB, Lemmens HJM. Lean body weight scalar for the anesthetic induction dose of propofol in morbidly obese subjects. Anesth Analg. 2011;113(1):57–62.

---

**Pierre O. Maitre** — clinical pharmacologist, University of Basel / Kantonsspital and later Inselspital Bern, Switzerland, with a period in Donald Stanski's group at Stanford; population pharmacokinetics of intravenous anesthetics

Pierre Maitre worked with Donald Stanski's anesthesia clinical-pharmacology group at Stanford, applying population pharmacokinetic methods (drawn in part from the mixed-effects modeling tradition of Lewis Sheiner and Samuel Vozeh) to anesthetic and sedative drugs. His most influential contribution characterized the population pharmacokinetics of alfentanil, pooling plasma-concentration data across multiple studies to define the average dose–concentration relationship and, critically, to quantify interindividual variability and the systematic effects of covariates such as age and body weight on clearance and distribution. This covariate-and-variability framing is precisely the structure that later model-based dosing and target-controlled infusion (TCI) systems require, and it is echoed in the covariate-driven parameterization used in stanpumpR.

Maitre also collaborated with Michael Bührer and Stanski on the quantitative electroencephalographic (EEG) pharmacodynamics of the benzodiazepines midazolam and diazepam, linking his population-PK expertise to effect-site/EEG PD modeling of drug effect. Together these lines of work helped establish the joint PK/PD and effect-site paradigm that underlies modern anesthetic simulation and closed-loop/TCI dosing.

*Key reference:* Maitre PO, Vozeh S, Heykants J, Thomson DA, Stanski DR. Population pharmacokinetics of alfentanil: the average dose-plasma concentration relationship and interindividual variability in patients. Anesthesiology. 1987;66(1):3–12.

---

**Jaap W. Mandema** — pharmacometrician; population PK/PD methodology, EEG pharmacodynamics, and drug-interaction modeling (later pharmacometrics consulting, Quantitative Solutions / Certara)

Jaap Mandema is a pharmacometrician whose early work modeled the central-nervous-system effects of sedative and anesthetic drugs using the EEG as a continuous, graded measure of drug effect. In doctoral work in the group of Meindert Danhof at the University of Leiden, he built PK/PD models of the benzodiazepine midazolam and its active metabolite α-hydroxymidazolam, using the sigmoid-Emax/effect-compartment framework to separate the contributions of parent drug and metabolite to measured EEG and behavioral effect — an early, rigorous treatment of active-metabolite pharmacodynamics.

Working with Lewis Sheiner and Davide Verotta at UCSF, and subsequently as an assistant professor in the Department of Anesthesia at Stanford, Mandema advanced the general methodology for building population PK/PD models, developing systematic, semiparametric approaches (empirical Bayes estimates regressed on covariates via generalized additive models) for detecting and incorporating covariate effects. This methodological program directly supports the covariate-based population models — age, weight, and other patient characteristics driving individualized PK/PD parameters — that TCI systems and stanpumpR rely on. Move the sentence to the end of the first (Leiden) paragraph, immediately after "— an early, rigorous treatment of active-metabolite pharmacodynamics.", and delete it from the second paragraph so that paragraph runs "...that TCI systems and stanpumpR rely on. He later became a leader in pharmacometrics consulting..." He later became a leader in pharmacometrics consulting (Quantitative Solutions, subsequently part of Certara), where he developed model-based meta-analysis for comparative efficacy and safety.

*Key references:* Mandema JW, Verotta D, Sheiner LB. Building population pharmacokinetic-pharmacodynamic models. I. Models for covariate effects. J Pharmacokinet Biopharm. 1992;20(5):511–528. • Mandema JW, Tuk B, van Steveninck AL, Breimer DD, Cohen AF, Danhof M. Pharmacokinetic-pharmacodynamic modeling of the central nervous system effects of midazolam and its main metabolite alpha-hydroxymidazolam in healthy volunteers. Clin Pharmacol Ther. 1992;51(6):715–728.

---

**Charles F. Minto** — anesthesiologist and pharmacometrician; research fellow with Steven Shafer at Stanford; co-developer of the remifentanil (Minto) model and of response-surface interaction modeling (later based in Sydney, Australia)

Minto, during his research fellowship at Stanford in Steven Shafer's laboratory (with Thomas Schnider), developed the population pharmacokinetic–pharmacodynamic model for remifentanil that bears his name and remains a standard model in target-controlled infusion (TCI) systems. The model characterized how age and lean body mass shift remifentanil disposition and effect, and introduced an age-dependent effect-site equilibration rate constant (ke0) linking plasma concentration to EEG effect. He later formalized the mathematics of anesthetic drug interactions, proposing a response-surface framework that extends single-drug sigmoid concentration–response relationships to combinations (e.g., propofol–opioid), which underlies the interaction modeling used in modern anesthesia simulation. Minto subsequently practiced in Sydney, Australia, and co-founded the Open TCI Initiative with Schnider.

*Key references:* Minto CF, Schnider TW, Egan TD, et al. Influence of age and gender on the pharmacokinetics and pharmacodynamics of remifentanil. I. Model development. Anesthesiology. 1997;86(1):10–23. • Minto CF, Schnider TW, Short TG, Gregg KM, Gentilini A, Shafer SL. Response surface model for anesthetic drug interactions. Anesthesiology. 2000;92(6):1603–1616.

---

**Lucian Radu-Radulescu** — pharmacodynamic-modeling collaborator on the Stanford-based Bouillon/Bruhn studies with Steven L. Shafer

Lucian Radu-Radulescu was a collaborator in Steven L. Shafer's Stanford group who contributed to its modeling of opioid-induced ventilatory depression and of propofol–opioid drug interaction. The name appears in the Bouillon et al. studies characterizing the ventilatory-depressant potency of remifentanil in the non–steady state and, in the interaction series, the pharmacodynamic interaction between propofol and remifentanil. The first study fit an indirect-response model to non-steady-state PaCO2 data to quantify the ventilatory-depressant potency of remifentanil alone (C50 for ventilatory depression 0.92 ng/mL); the second used response-surface methods to quantify the propofol-remifentanil interaction for hypnosis, tolerance of laryngoscopy, bispectral index, and EEG approximate entropy. The documented contribution is as a co-author on these interaction/ventilation modeling papers; the independent publication record under this name is limited, so the entry is scoped accordingly.

*Key references:* Bouillon T, Bruhn J, Radu-Radulescu L, Andresen C, Cohane C, Shafer SL. A model of the ventilatory depressant potency of remifentanil in the non–steady state. Anesthesiology. 2003;99(4):779–787. • Bouillon TW, Bruhn J, Radulescu L, Andresen C, Shafer TJ, Cohane C, Shafer SL. Pharmacodynamic interaction between propofol and remifentanil regarding hypnosis, tolerance of laryngoscopy, bispectral index, and electroencephalographic approximate entropy. Anesthesiology. 2004;100(6):1353–1372.

**Thomas W. Schnider** — anesthesiologist; research fellow with Steven Shafer at Stanford; developer of the Schnider propofol PK/PD model widely used for TCI (later head of the Institute for Anaesthesiology, Kantonsspital St. Gallen, Switzerland)

Schnider, during his research fellowship at Stanford in Steven Shafer's laboratory (with Charles Minto), derived the covariate-based propofol pharmacokinetic and pharmacodynamic models that are among the most widely implemented in commercial effect-site TCI pumps. The pharmacokinetic study defined how method of administration and covariates (age, weight, height, lean body mass) influence propofol disposition, and the companion pharmacodynamic study quantified the influence of age on propofol effect (C50 for loss of consciousness falling from 2.35 to 1.25 µg/mL between ages 25 and 75) and estimated a single, age-independent plasma–effect-site equilibration rate constant (ke0 = 0.456 min⁻¹, time to peak effect ≈1.6–1.7 min), enabling effect-site targeting. He later became head of the Institute for Anaesthesiology at Kantonsspital St. Gallen, Switzerland, and co-founded the Open TCI Initiative with Minto.

*Key references:* Schnider TW, Minto CF, Gambus PL, et al. The influence of method of administration and covariates on the pharmacokinetics of propofol in adult volunteers. Anesthesiology. 1998;88(5):1170–1182. • Schnider TW, Minto CF, Shafer SL, et al. The influence of age on propofol pharmacodynamics. Anesthesiology. 1999;90(6):1502–1516.

---

**Steven L. Shafer** — anesthesiologist and pharmacologist; author of stanpumpR and the original STANPUMP infusion program; Professor Emeritus of Anesthesiology, Perioperative and Pain Medicine, Stanford University

Steven Shafer is known for translating anesthetic PK/PD theory into working drug-delivery tools. In the late 1980s he wrote STANPUMP (STANford infusion PUMP), a computer program that drove infusion pumps to achieve and maintain user-specified plasma or effect-site concentrations of intravenous anesthetics — an implementation of target-controlled infusion (TCI) built on closed-form solutions to multi-compartment models. He placed STANPUMP in the public domain, and it became the standard research platform for target-controlled infusion, used to develop and validate many of the pharmacokinetic models later implemented in commercial TCI pumps. With Keith Gregg, he published the control algorithms for rapidly achieving and maintaining stable effect-site concentrations, extending TCI from plasma targeting to effect-site targeting using the ke0 parameter. He is also the author of stanpumpR, the open-source R/Shiny successor to this line of work, which uses the same closed-form compartmental mathematics to simulate plasma and effect-site concentrations.

Shafer's research spans opioid and hypnotic pharmacology, population modeling, and the pharmacokinetic concepts clinicians use to reason about infusion regimens — including context-sensitive decrement times and rational drug selection based on predicted concentration trajectories. He has also been influential in research integrity and publication ethics, including a long tenure as Editor-in-Chief of Anesthesia & Analgesia.

**Jacques Somma** — anesthesiologist; research fellow with Steven L. Shafer at Stanford (later Université Laval, Québec)

Jacques Somma was a research fellow with Steven L. Shafer at Stanford, where he worked on the population pharmacokinetics and pharmacodynamics of sedative and anesthetic agents delivered by computer-controlled (target-controlled) infusion. With Katie Zomorodi and colleagues he carried out a paired set of studies on midazolam sedation in cardiac surgical patients following coronary artery bypass grafting: Somma led the pharmacodynamic analysis, modeling the concentration–sedation relationship in the surgical ICU, *Key references:* Somma J, Donner A, Zomorodi K, Sladen R, Ramsay J, Geller E, Shafer SL. Population pharmacodynamics of midazolam administered by target controlled infusion in SICU patients after CABG surgery. Anesthesiology. 1998;89(6):1430–1443. • Zomorodi K, Donner A, Somma J, Barr J, Sladen R, Ramsay J, Geller E, Shafer SL. Population pharmacokinetics of midazolam administered by target controlled infusion for sedation following coronary artery bypass grafting. Anesthesiology. 1998;89(6):1418–1429.. This work is frequently cited in the context of ICU sedation modeling and the clinical pharmacology of midazolam infusions. He subsequently returned to Canada and has practiced and taught anesthesiology at Université Laval in Québec City.

*Key reference:* Somma J, Donner A, Zomorodi K, Sladen R, Ramsay J, Geller E, Shafer SL. Population pharmacodynamics of midazolam administered by target controlled infusion in SICU patients after CABG surgery. Anesthesiology. 1998;89(6):1430–1443.

---

**Donald R. Stanski** — anesthesiologist and clinical pharmacologist, Professor (Emeritus) of Anesthesia

Donald Stanski helped establish the rigorous, model-based study of intravenous anesthetic drugs. A recurring theme of his work is the use of the processed electroencephalogram (EEG) as a continuous, quantifiable measure of anesthetic drug effect, allowing pharmacodynamics to be modeled with the same precision as pharmacokinetics. His collaboration with Lewis Sheiner established the effect-compartment model as the standard tool of anesthetic PK/PD analysis (see University of California, San Francisco), linking plasma concentration to drug effect through ke0 and providing the conceptual basis for effect-site targeting.

Stanski applied simultaneous and population PK/PD methods (including NONMEM) to the anesthetic agents themselves — notably thiopental, fentanyl, and alfentanil — and showed that the mechanism of the age-related fall in dose requirement differs by drug. For fentanyl and alfentanil it is pharmacodynamic: brain sensitivity, measured by the EEG, increases with age while the pharmacokinetics are essentially unchanged. For thiopental his re-analysis with Maitre found no age-related change in brain responsiveness and traced the reduced dose requirement instead to a pharmacokinetic change — a roughly 27% decline in rapid intercompartment clearance between ages 35 and 80. His mentorship and collaboration at Stanford — including work with Steven Shafer on computer-controlled infusion — connected quantitative pharmacology to bedside drug delivery, and he later carried these principles into pharmaceutical drug development and regulatory science.

*Key reference:* Stanski DR, Maitre PO. Population pharmacokinetics and pharmacodynamics of thiopental: the effect of age revisited. Anesthesiology. 1990;72(3):412–422.

---

**John R. Varvel** — anesthesiologist; Stanford University anesthesia pharmacology group, later Lincoln Anesthesiology Group and Saint Elizabeth Regional Medical Center (now CHI Health St. Elizabeth), Lincoln, Nebraska; developer of standardized performance metrics for computer-controlled infusion pumps

John Varvel, working with the Stanford statistician David L. Donoho and with Steven L. Shafer, addressed a foundational methodological problem in target-controlled infusion: how to quantify, in a statistically sound and clinically interpretable way, how well a computer-controlled infusion pump achieves its target concentrations. Their 1992 paper defined a now-standard set of performance measures based on the performance error between predicted and measured drug concentrations — median performance error (MDPE, a measure of bias), median absolute performance error (MDAPE, a measure of inaccuracy), divergence (drift over time), and wobble (intra-individual variability).

These four metrics became the accepted vocabulary for validating and comparing pharmacokinetic models and TCI devices, and they remain the reporting standard in prospective TCI model-validation studies today.

*Key reference:* Varvel JR, Donoho DL, Shafer SL. Measuring the predictive performance of computer-controlled infusion pumps. J Pharmacokinet Biopharm. 1992;20(1):63–94.

---

**D. Russell Wada** — pharmacometrician; physiologically based PK modeling of anesthetics and population PK (Stanford Dept. of Anesthesia during the anesthesia-modeling era; later Pharsight/Certara)

Russ Wada received his PhD from UCLA (1991) and completed a postdoctoral fellowship at Stanford University in Donald Stanski's anesthesia pharmacology group, working with William F. Ebling, and subsequently served as a research associate in the Stanford Department of Anesthesia. In that period he developed physiologically based pharmacokinetic models of intravenous anesthetics — most notably thiopental — that describe drug behavior in terms of tissue blood flows, tissue masses, and organ clearances rather than abstract compartments. This physiologic framing captures the first-pass and early-distribution phase that governs the rapid rise and fall of anesthetic concentrations after an IV bolus, and it allowed simulation of how altered cardiac output and body composition change thiopental disposition. His work connected to the broader recirculatory-modeling community, including the Northwestern group (Krejcie, Avram, Henthorn).

After academia, Wada moved into pharmacometrics consulting, joining Pharsight Corporation in 1997, moving in 2005 to Quantitative Solutions — later part of Certara, where he became a senior vice president — and more recently to QuanTx Consulting, becoming a recognized leader in model-based drug development across many therapeutic areas.

*Key reference:* Wada DR, Björkman S, Ebling WF, Harashima H, Harapat SR, Stanski DR. Computer simulation of the effects of alterations in blood flows and body composition on thiopental pharmacokinetics in humans. Anesthesiology. 1997;87(4):884–899.

---

**Elizabeth J. Youngs** — anesthesiologist and research fellow, Stanford University (Shafer laboratory)

Elizabeth J. Youngs trained as a research fellow with Steven L. Shafer at Stanford, where she worked on the pharmacokinetic and pharmacodynamic basis of recovery from intravenous anesthetics and opioids. Her most influential contribution is a 1994 analysis with Shafer that reframed how clinicians think about offset of opioid effect: rather than relying on the terminal elimination half-life, the work simulated three-compartment models of fentanyl, alfentanil, and sufentanil to determine which primary pharmacokinetic parameters govern the 20%, 50%, and 80% "decrement times" — showing that a small central volume and a large elimination clearance always speed recovery, whereas larger peripheral volumes and intercompartmental clearances help only after short infusions and small decrements and hurt after long infusions and large ones. This "decrement time" framing is the conceptual companion to the context-sensitive half-time and remains a standard tool for comparing recovery profiles among opioids.

Youngs was also a co-author on the landmark Schnider propofol pharmacokinetic study conducted with the Stanford group and collaborators in Bern, which characterized the influence of dosing method and patient covariates on propofol disposition and underpins the widely used "Schnider" target-controlled infusion model.

*Key references:* Youngs EJ, Shafer SL. Pharmacokinetic parameters relevant to recovery from opioids. Anesthesiology. 1994;81(4):833–842. • Schnider TW, Minto CF, Gambus PL, Andresen C, Goodale DB, Shafer SL, Youngs EJ. The influence of method of administration and covariates on the pharmacokinetics of propofol in adult volunteers. Anesthesiology. 1998;88(5):1170–1182.

---

**Katie Zomorodi** — pharmacometrician; research fellow with Steven L. Shafer at Stanford (later industry pharmacometrics)

Katayoun (Katie) Zomorodi was a fellow in Steven L. Shafer's laboratory at Stanford, contributing to the group's population modeling of intravenous sedatives. With Jacques Somma and colleagues she authored the population pharmacokinetic half of the paired midazolam target-controlled infusion studies in post-cardiac-surgery patients, quantifying midazolam disposition during prolonged sedation in the surgical ICU. She subsequently pursued a career in clinical pharmacology and pharmacometrics in the pharmaceutical industry.

*Key reference:* Zomorodi K, Donner A, Somma J, Barr J, Sladen R, Ramsay J, Geller E, Shafer SL. Population pharmacokinetics of midazolam administered by target controlled infusion for sedation following coronary artery bypass grafting. Anesthesiology. 1998;89(6):1418–1429.

## Stellenbosch University (South Africa)

**Johan F. Coetzee** — anesthesiologist; Professor of Anaesthesiology, Department of Anaesthesiology and Critical Care, Stellenbosch University; clinical evaluation of propofol pharmacokinetic parameter sets for target-controlled infusion

Coetzee is known for rigorous clinical evaluation of propofol pharmacokinetic parameter sets for target-controlled infusion. His widely cited study randomly allocated 30 patients to have their propofol TCI driven by one of three pharmacokinetic parameter sets — Marsh, Tackley, or Dyck — and quantified the bias and inaccuracy each introduced into predicted plasma concentrations, informing model selection for propofol TCI systems. His broader research includes pharmacokinetics and pharmacodynamics in cardiac anesthesia and the clinical application of TCI.

*Key reference:* Coetzee JF, Glen JB, Wium CA, Boshoff L. Pharmacokinetic model selection for target controlled infusions of propofol: assessment of three parameter sets. Anesthesiology. 1995;82(6):1328–1345.

---

## Universidad Católica de Chile & Clínica Alemana (Santiago)

**Luis Ignacio Cortínez** — anesthesiologist and pharmacometrician, Pontificia Universidad Católica de Chile; population PK/PD, TCI, and allometric scaling

Cortínez is a leading figure in the Latin-American TCI/PK community and an internationally recognized population pharmacokineticist. His work applies nonlinear mixed-effects modeling and theory-based allometric scaling — using fat-free mass and normal fat mass as size descriptors — to explain how body weight and composition alter drug disposition, with particular attention to obesity. He has built and evaluated population models for dexmedetomidine, ketamine, and propofol, and has contributed extensively to the methodology of covariate scaling in anesthetic PK.

He collaborates closely with pharmacometricians such as Brian J. Anderson and Nicholas Holford, and with the Chilean anesthesia group including Pablo Sepúlveda. His obesity-focused models are widely cited in guidance on dosing anesthetics and sedatives in obese patients.

*Key reference:* Cortínez LI, Anderson BJ, Holford NHG, Puga V, de la Fuente N, Auad H, et al. Dexmedetomidine pharmacokinetics in the obese. Eur J Clin Pharmacol. 2015;71(12):1501–1508.

---

**Pablo O. Sepúlveda Voullième** — anesthesiologist, Clínica Alemana de Santiago, Chile; propofol TCI, effect-site pharmacodynamics, and ke0 estimation

Sepúlveda is a Chilean anesthesiologist known for critical, clinically grounded investigation of effect-site (ke0) modeling in propofol TCI. His work examines how the plasma–effect-site equilibration rate constant behaves under different infusion speeds and how age influences effect-site targeting, and he has argued for careful re-evaluation of the effect-site model as implemented in propofol PK/PD models (including the Eleveld model). This line of work bears directly on how TCI pumps translate a target concentration into loss and recovery of consciousness.

He collaborates with Luis Ignacio Cortínez and other members of the Chilean PK/PD community, contributing to the Latin-American body of TCI research and to ongoing debate over the correct parameterization of propofol effect-site kinetics.

*Key reference:* Sepúlveda PO, Cortínez LI, Recart A, Muñoz HR. Predictive ability of propofol effect-site concentrations during fast and slow infusion rates. Acta Anaesthesiol Scand. 2010;54(4):447–452.

---

## University Medical Center Groningen (Netherlands)

**Anthony R. Absalom** — anesthesiologist; Professor of Anesthesiology, UMC Groningen

Absalom is a leading investigator in TCI, closed-loop anesthesia, and propofol/remifentanil clinical pharmacology. Early in his career at Glasgow (with Gavin Kenny) he reported closed-loop control of propofol anesthesia using the Bispectral Index as the feedback variable, and he was closely involved in the "Paedfusor," a pediatric propofol TCI system incorporating a child-specific pharmacokinetic data set, whose accuracy he evaluated in children undergoing cardiac surgery or catheterization. At Groningen he has collaborated closely with Michel Struys.

Absalom co-authored (with Douglas Eleveld and Struys) the Eleveld "general-purpose" propofol PK/PD model, developed to apply across broad populations from children to the elderly and now widely implemented in TCI devices. He is also a prolific author and editor of the TCI and intravenous-anesthesia literature.

*Key references:* Absalom AR, Sutcliffe N, Kenny GN. Closed-loop control of anesthesia using Bispectral index: performance assessment in patients undergoing major orthopedic surgery under combined general and regional anesthesia. Anesthesiology. 2002;96(1):67–73. • Eleveld DJ, Colin P, Absalom AR, Struys MMRF. Pharmacokinetic–pharmacodynamic model for propofol for broad application in anaesthesia and sedation. Br J Anaesth. 2018;120(5):942–959.

---

**Douglas J. Eleveld** — pharmacometrician; general-purpose ("Eleveld") propofol and remifentanil PK/PD models spanning all ages

Eleveld, with Michel Struys, Anthony Absalom, and colleagues at Groningen, developed general-purpose ("all-in-one") pharmacokinetic–pharmacodynamic models intended to apply across the entire patient spectrum — from neonates to the elderly, and from underweight to morbidly obese — rather than being restricted to a narrow population. His propofol PK/PD model, built by pooling data from many prior studies and using bispectral index (BIS) as the effect endpoint, and his allometric remifentanil model, using age, weight, and sex as covariates, have been increasingly adopted in modern TCI systems as unified alternatives to the older Marsh, Schnider, and Minto models. These models incorporate effect-site (ke0) parameterization for effect-site–targeted infusion.

*Key references:* Eleveld DJ, Proost JH, Vereecke H, et al. An allometric model of remifentanil pharmacokinetics and pharmacodynamics. Anesthesiology. 2017;126(6):1005–1018. • Eleveld DJ, Colin P, Absalom AR, Struys MMRF. Pharmacokinetic–pharmacodynamic model for propofol for broad application in anaesthesia and sedation. Br J Anaesth. 2018;120(5):942–959.

---

**Michel M. R. F. Struys** — anesthesiologist; Professor and Chair of Anesthesiology, UMC Groningen (Netherlands); also Professor, Department of Basic and Applied Medical Sciences, Ghent University (Belgium)

Struys is a central figure in the development and clinical validation of target-controlled infusion (TCI) and automated ("closed-loop") anesthesia. Working at Ghent University with biomedical engineer Tom De Smet, he co-developed the RUGLOOP TCI and closed-loop research software and reported one of the first patient-individualized, model-based, adaptive closed-loop systems that used the Bispectral Index (BIS) as the controlled variable to titrate propofol. His group's work spans effect-site (Ce) targeting, characterization of propofol pharmacodynamics and drug interactions, and comparative evaluation of infusion strategies against manual control.

His later collaborations extended this line of work to Bayesian controllers that refine the patient's own pharmacokinetic model from measured effect during the case, and to combined propofol–remifentanil closed-loop coadministration. After moving to Groningen he continued as a leading investigator in TCI and closed-loop control, frequently publishing alongside Anthony Absalom, and contributed to development and validation of general-purpose propofol PK/PD models used in modern TCI.

*Key reference:* Struys MMRF, De Smet T, Versichelen LFM, Van de Velde S, Van den Broecke R, Mortier EP. Comparison of closed-loop controlled administration of propofol using Bispectral Index as the controlled variable versus "standard practice" controlled administration. Anesthesiology. 2001;95(1):6–17.

## University of Alabama at Birmingham

**J. Michael Alvis** — biomedical engineer and anesthesiology investigator; principal developer of the CACI (computer-assisted continuous infusion) system

Michael Alvis was the engineer who, with J. Gerald Reves at the University of Alabama at Birmingham, built one of the first practical computer-assisted continuous infusion systems for intravenous anesthetics. The CACI system used a pharmacokinetic model of fentanyl to compute the infusion-rate schedule needed to rapidly reach and then hold a target plasma concentration, and to let the anesthesiologist raise or lower that target interactively during surgery. In a controlled comparison in 30 cardiac surgical patients, CACI held measured plasma fentanyl close to the predicted target (measured/predicted ratios 0.99 and 1.08) and, in the adjustable-target arm, produced greater hemodynamic stability and fewer adjuvant drug interventions than manual bolus administration; the authors concluded the computer-assisted method was safe and as good as the manual one.

This work is widely regarded as a foundational proof of concept for target-controlled infusion. Alvis also described the interactive control system in the engineering literature, establishing the model-driven infusion architecture later refined into systems such as STANPUMP and the commercial "Diprifusor."

*Key references:* Alvis JM, Reves JG, Govier AV, Menkhaus PG, Henling CE, Spain JA, Bradley E. Computer-assisted continuous infusions of fentanyl during cardiac anesthesia: comparison with a manual method. Anesthesiology. 1985;63(1):41–49. • Alvis JM, Reves JG, Spain JA, Sheppard LC. Computer-assisted continuous infusion of the intravenous analgesic fentanyl during general anesthesia — an interactive system. IEEE Trans Biomed Eng. 1985;32(5):323–329.
