## University of Auckland (New Zealand)

**Brian J. Anderson** — pediatric anesthesiologist and clinical pharmacologist, University of Auckland; allometric size-and-maturation modeling for drug dosing in children

Brian Anderson is a leading figure in pediatric clinical pharmacology, known for applying quantitative population PK/PD methods to drug dosing in children and neonates. His central contribution, developed in close collaboration with Nicholas Holford, is the theory-based (allometric) approach to describing how a child's size and maturity jointly govern drug clearance and volume. In this framework, clearance is scaled to body weight using a fixed ¾-power allometric exponent (and volume with an exponent of 1), referenced to a standard 70-kg adult, while a separate sigmoid (Emax) maturation function of postmenstrual age captures the ontogeny of clearance pathways in the fetus, neonate, and infant. Separating size from maturity in this mechanistic way lets a single model span the neonate-to-adult range without empirical per-age-band adjustments.

Anderson has applied these principles across many agents relevant to anesthesia and analgesia, including paracetamol/acetaminophen, propofol, opioids, and dexmedetomidine, building population models that inform rational pediatric dosing. His work with Holford established postmenstrual age (rather than postnatal age) as the appropriate maturational descriptor and demonstrated the practical value of standardized allometric scaling for extrapolating adult pharmacokinetics to the very young.

These size-and-maturation methods are foundational to modern general-purpose and target-controlled infusion (TCI) models: the Eleveld propofol model, for example, uses allometric scaling and maturation functions to cover neonates through elderly adults in one model, and the Chilean group led by Luis Ignacio Cortínez and Pablo Sepúlveda (frequent Anderson collaborators) has extended allometric propofol and dexmedetomidine modeling, including in obesity.

*Key reference:* Anderson BJ, Holford NHG. Mechanism-based concepts of size and maturity in pharmacokinetics. Annu Rev Pharmacol Toxicol. 2008;48:303–332.

---

**Nicholas H. G. Holford** — clinical pharmacologist and pharmacometrician, University of Auckland; PK/PD principles and allometric size standardization

Nicholas Holford is a foundational figure in pharmacometrics whose work shaped the modern quantitative understanding of the dose–concentration–effect relationship. His early collaboration with Lewis B. Sheiner at the University of California, San Francisco produced one of the most influential syntheses in the field, showing how pharmacokinetic and pharmacodynamic models are linked and clinically applied — including Sheiner's effect-compartment (link) model, which connects plasma concentration to the site of drug effect and is a cornerstone of anesthetic PK/PD and TCI design. This dose–concentration–effect framework, together with the NONMEM-based nonlinear mixed-effects (population) methods that Holford applied, extended, and did much to popularize, underlies much of contemporary model-based drug development and individualized dosing.

Holford's proposal of a standardized allometric size standard for pharmacokinetics — scaling clearance and volume to a 70-kg reference using fixed theory-based exponents — gave the field a consistent, mechanistically motivated way to handle body size across the age and weight spectrum. In partnership with Brian Anderson, he extended this into the combined size-plus-maturation paradigm now standard in pediatric pharmacology. His broader contributions also include disease-progression modeling and time-to-event (survival) methods in pharmacometrics.

These principles feed directly into modern anesthetic dosing tools: general-purpose TCI models such as Eleveld's propofol model rely on Holford-style allometric scaling and maturation, and the Chilean group (Cortínez, Sepúlveda) has built on the same foundations for propofol and dexmedetomidine. Holford's size standard and PK/PD framework remain reference points for how covariates are handled in population models throughout anesthesia.

*Key references:* Holford NHG, Sheiner LB. Understanding the dose-effect relationship: clinical application of pharmacokinetic-pharmacodynamic models. Clin Pharmacokinet. 1981;6(6):429–453. • Holford NHG. A size standard for pharmacokinetics. Clin Pharmacokinet. 1996;30(5):329–332.

---

**Timothy G. Short** — anaesthetist, Auckland City Hospital and the University of Auckland; anesthetic drug interactions and depth-of-anaesthesia trials

Timothy Short is a specialist anaesthetist at Auckland City Hospital and honorary professor in the Department of Anaesthesiology at the University of Auckland. His doctoral work was in benzodiazepine pharmacology, and his early clinical pharmacology established the quantitative shape of hypnotic–hypnotic and hypnotic–opioid interaction. In a study of 400 female patients performed while he was at the Chinese University of Hong Kong, Short, Plummer and Chui determined quantal dose–response curves for midazolam, propofol and alfentanil given alone and in combination, at endpoints of hypnosis and of anaesthesia — although at the anaesthesia endpoint no dose-related effect could be demonstrated for midazolam or alfentanil given alone. Every two-drug pair was synergistic for the hypnotic endpoint — the observed ED50 fell well below the additive prediction — while the three-drug combination produced less effect than the individual drugs and their pairwise interactions would predict, an early demonstration that a three-drug anaesthetic interaction cannot be predicted by adding up the pairwise interactions.

That line of work led directly into response-surface modeling. Short was a co-author of the landmark paper by Minto, Schnider, Short, Gregg, Gentilini and Shafer, which replaced single-endpoint isobolographic description with a continuous surface over the full concentration plane, allowing additivity, synergy and antagonism to be expressed as one parameterized model and combined with pharmacokinetics to predict effect over time. Working with Shafer's group at the Palo Alto VA, he then addressed the practical problem the surfaces created — how to estimate them without impossibly large studies — publishing an efficient trial design for eliciting a PK/PD model-based interaction surface between two intravenous anaesthetics. He later closed the loop to delivery, showing with Hannam, Merry and colleagues that a propofol–remifentanil response surface for bispectral index could drive a pharmacodynamic target-controlled infusion targeting the combined drug effect rather than either drug's concentration.

Short is also known for large randomized trials of depth-of-anaesthesia titration. He was, with Kate Leslie, a principal investigator of the BALANCED anaesthesia study, an international trial that randomized patients aged 60 and over at increased surgical risk to light (BIS 50) or deep (BIS 35) general anaesthesia and found no evidence that light anaesthesia improved one-year survival. He is a past chairman of the executive of the ANZCA Clinical Trials Network and remains active in multicentre perioperative trials.

*Key references:* Short TG, Plummer JL, Chui PT. Hypnotic and anaesthetic interactions between midazolam, propofol and alfentanil. Br J Anaesth. 1992;69(2):162–167. • Minto CF, Schnider TW, Short TG, Gregg KM, Gentilini A, Shafer SL. Response surface model for anesthetic drug interactions. Anesthesiology. 2000;92(6):1603–1616.

---

## University of California, San Francisco (UCSF)

**Stuart L. Beal** — biostatistician; co-developer of NONMEM and nonlinear mixed-effects (population) pharmacokinetics

Stuart Beal earned his PhD in biostatistics from UCLA (1973) and spent his career as a professor of biostatistics at UCSF, where his decades-long partnership with clinical pharmacologist Lewis B. Sheiner produced the population approach to pharmacokinetics and its enduring software embodiment, NONMEM (NONlinear Mixed Effects Modeling). The Beal–Sheiner framework treats sparse, unbalanced clinical data from many subjects as a single analysis, simultaneously estimating typical (fixed-effect) parameter values, their covariate dependencies, and the random inter-individual and residual variability. This reframing — modeling the population rather than fitting each patient separately — became the methodological foundation of modern pharmacometrics and model-informed drug development.

Beal was primarily responsible for the statistical estimation machinery underlying NONMEM, including the first-order (FO) method and, later, the first-order conditional estimation (FOCE) methods that improved accuracy when data are informative about individual parameters. His authorship of the successive NONMEM Users Guides made these estimation algorithms usable across pharmacology and industry, where NONMEM remains a de facto standard. In anesthesia, the population approach he and Sheiner established underpins the covariate-based PK models and TCI parameter sets used to dose intravenous anesthetics and opioids. Stuart Beal passed away in 2006.

*Key references:* Beal SL, Sheiner LB. Estimating population kinetics. Crit Rev Biomed Eng. 1982;8(3):195–222. • Beal SL, Sheiner LB, Boeckmann AJ, eds. NONMEM Users Guides, Parts I–VIII. San Francisco: NONMEM Project Group, University of California, San Francisco; 1989–1998 (later editions, Icon Development Solutions, Ellicott City, MD, 2009).

---

**Leslie Z. Benet** — professor emeritus of bioengineering and therapeutic sciences, UCSF; clearance theory, noncompartmental analysis, and bioavailability science

Benet is among the most influential figures in modern pharmacokinetics. A UCSF PhD in pharmaceutical chemistry, he joined the School of Pharmacy faculty and served from 1978 to 1998 as the third chair of its Department of Pharmacy, succeeding Sidney Riegelman; during and after his tenure the department was renamed the Department of Biopharmaceutical Sciences and then the Department of Bioengineering and Therapeutic Sciences. He was a founder and the first president of the American Association of Pharmaceutical Scientists, president of the APhA Academy of Pharmaceutical Sciences and of the American Association of Colleges of Pharmacy, and was elected to the National Academy of Medicine. He has supervised more than 55 doctoral theses and 100 postdoctoral fellows.

His most durable contribution to the mathematics used by simulation tools such as this one is the noncompartmental, statistical-moment treatment of drug disposition. With Renato L. Galeazzi he showed that the steady-state volume of distribution can be obtained model-independently from the zeroth and first moments of the concentration–time curve (Vss = dose × AUMC/AUC² after intravenous administration), together with mean residence time — parameters that require no assumption about the number of compartments. That paper became the most-cited article in the *Journal of Pharmaceutical Sciences*. Benet also argued for clearance as the primary, physiologically anchored pharmacokinetic parameter, shaped the science of bioavailability and bioequivalence (advising the FDA on its guidances), demonstrated that intestinal metabolism and transport, not the liver alone, gate oral drug entry, and with Chi-Yuan Wu proposed the Biopharmaceutics Drug Disposition Classification System (BDDCS), which extends the Biopharmaceutics Classification System to predict metabolizing-enzyme and transporter interplay. He remains a prominent and deliberately contrarian voice in the long-running debate over hepatic clearance models, arguing that organ clearance relationships follow from Kirchhoff's laws independently of any particular anatomic model such as the well-stirred or parallel-tube formulations — a position that continues to be actively contested.

Benet's UCSF connections run directly into anesthesia pharmacology. His department was the academic home of Lewis Sheiner and Stuart Beal, whose effect-compartment (ke0) model and NONMEM population-modeling methodology together underpin the pharmacodynamic models and target-controlled infusion systems used in anesthesia. With Sheiner he co-authored the "Design and Optimization of Dosage Regimens: Pharmacokinetic Data" appendix in *Goodman & Gilman's The Pharmacological Basis of Therapeutics*, for many years a standard clinical source of pharmacokinetic parameters. With Carl Peck, William Barr and others he co-authored the 1992 consensus paper on integrating pharmacokinetics, pharmacodynamics and toxicokinetics into rational drug development, which helped make exposure–response modeling a regulatory expectation rather than an academic exercise. His own laboratory work is not anesthesia-specific, but the clearance, volume and residence-time concepts he formalized are the vocabulary in which anesthetic pharmacokinetic models are written.

*Key references:* Benet LZ, Galeazzi RL. Noncompartmental determination of the steady-state volume of distribution. J Pharm Sci. 1979;68(8):1071–1074. • Wu CY, Benet LZ. Predicting drug disposition via application of BCS: transport/absorption/elimination interplay and development of a biopharmaceutics drug disposition classification system. Pharm Res. 2005;22(1):11–23.

---

**Edmund I. "Ted" Eger II** — anesthesiologist and inhaled-anesthetic pharmacologist; originator of the Minimum Alveolar Concentration (MAC) standard

Ted Eger was the defining figure in the pharmacology of inhaled (volatile) anesthetics. Joining the UCSF faculty in 1960, he originated and standardized the concept of Minimum Alveolar Concentration (MAC) — the alveolar concentration of an inhaled anesthetic, at one atmosphere, that prevents movement in response to a noxious stimulus in 50% of subjects. MAC became, and remains, the universal measure of inhaled-anesthetic potency and the common currency for comparing agents and dosing them clinically.

MAC was first defined in dogs with Giles Merkel (Anesthesiology 1963;24:346–357) and then extended to humans and established as a potency standard with Lawrence J. Saidman, then a UCSF research fellow, and Bernard Brandstater, the founding chair of anesthesiology at the American University of Beirut who worked with the UCSF group. Beyond potency, Eger characterized the uptake, distribution, and elimination kinetics of volatile anesthetics — how factors such as blood:gas and tissue solubility, ventilation, and cardiac output govern the speed of anesthetic onset and recovery. He applied this framework to the early human pharmacology of successive agents including halothane, isoflurane, desflurane, and sevoflurane, publishing more than 500 peer-reviewed papers over his career. Ted Eger passed away in 2017.

*Key reference:* Eger EI 2nd, Saidman LJ, Brandstater B. Minimum alveolar anesthetic concentration: a standard of anesthetic potency. Anesthesiology. 1965;26(6):756–763.

---

**Dennis M. Fisher** — anesthesiologist and pharmacometrician, Professor Emeritus of Anesthesia

Dennis Fisher is a clinical pharmacologist recognized for methodological rigor in anesthetic PK/PD analysis and for extending compartmental modeling into pediatric anesthesia. Much of his work characterized the pharmacokinetics and pharmacodynamics of neuromuscular blocking drugs — including vecuronium, atracurium, and pancuronium — across the age spectrum from neonates to adults, clarifying how developmental changes in body composition and clearance alter dosing. His analyses of atracurium elimination quantified the relative contributions of Hofmann degradation, ester hydrolysis, and organ-based clearance.

Fisher used PK/PD simulation to explain clinically important but counterintuitive phenomena — for example, why recovery time lengthens disproportionately after larger or repeated relaxant doses — demonstrating how the interaction of pharmacokinetics with a sigmoid concentration-effect relationship shapes the observed time course of drug effect. Beyond his own studies, he served as a reviewer at the FDA's Center for Drug Evaluation and Research, an editor at Anesthesiology, and a widely cited educator on statistical and pharmacometric methods in anesthesia research.

*Key references:* Fisher DM, Rosen JI. A pharmacokinetic explanation for increasing recovery time following larger or repeated doses of nondepolarizing muscle relaxants. Anesthesiology. 1986;65(3):286–291. • Fisher DM, Canfell PC, Fahey MR, et al. Elimination of atracurium in humans: contribution of Hofmann elimination and ester hydrolysis versus organ-based elimination. Anesthesiology. 1986;65(1):6–12.

---

**Lawrence J. Saidman** — anesthesiologist; co-originator of the Minimum Alveolar Concentration (MAC) concept, University of California, San Francisco (UCSF)

Lawrence J. Saidman was a foundational figure in the quantitative pharmacology of inhaled anesthetics. As a resident and young investigator at UCSF in the early-to-mid 1960s, he worked with Edmund I. "Ted" Eger II and Bernard Brandstater to define and validate Minimum Alveolar Concentration (MAC) — the alveolar concentration of an inhaled anesthetic at which half of subjects fail to move in response to a standardized noxious stimulus. By anchoring anesthetic potency to a reproducible, physiologically grounded endpoint, MAC transformed inhaled-anesthetic dosing from an empirical art into a measurable standard, and it remains the universal yardstick of volatile-anesthetic potency to this day.

Saidman's early work extended MAC beyond a single-agent measurement into a quantitative framework. With Eger he characterized how nitrous oxide and narcotic premedication reduce the alveolar halothane concentration required for anesthesia, establishing the additive, quantifiable nature of anesthetic and adjuvant effects that underlies modern balanced anesthesia. This body of work helped launch a durable UCSF-centered tradition of rigorous inhaled-anesthetic pharmacokinetics and pharmacodynamics.

After the foundational UCSF period, Saidman moved to the University of California, San Diego (UCSD) and later to Stanford University, where he became Professor of Anesthesia (subsequently Emeritus). He was also a long-serving Editor-in-Chief of the journal Anesthesiology, shaping the discipline's leading peer-reviewed literature for many years. Lawrence Saidman passed away in 2026.

*Key references:* Saidman LJ, Eger EI 2nd. Effect of nitrous oxide and of narcotic premedication on the alveolar concentration of halothane required for anesthesia. Anesthesiology. 1964;25(3):302–306. • Eger EI 2nd, Saidman LJ, Brandstater B. Minimum alveolar anesthetic concentration: a standard of anesthetic potency. Anesthesiology. 1965;26(6):756–763.

---

**Lewis B. Sheiner** — physician-pharmacologist; co-founder of population pharmacokinetics and pharmacometrics

Lewis Sheiner was a foundational figure in quantitative clinical pharmacology whose methods underlie essentially all modern anesthetic PK/PD modeling. With statistician Stuart L. Beal at UCSF, he developed the nonlinear mixed-effects modeling framework and its software implementation, NONMEM, which made it possible to estimate population pharmacokinetic parameters — and the between-subject and residual variability around them — from sparse, routinely collected clinical data rather than dense experimental sampling. This "population approach" became the standard for characterizing how covariates such as age, weight, and organ function shift drug disposition, and it is the statistical engine behind the population models stanpumpR uses.

In anesthesia specifically, Sheiner's collaboration with Donald Stanski established the effect-compartment (link) model as the standard tool of anesthetic PK/PD analysis, through their simultaneous modeling of d-tubocurarine; a closely related effect-compartment model had been described independently by Hull and colleagues for pancuronium the previous year. By positing a hypothetical effect site connected to plasma by a first-order rate constant (ke0), they explained the temporal lag (hysteresis) between plasma concentration and observed drug effect, and made it possible to fit pharmacokinetics and pharmacodynamics simultaneously. The effect-site concentration and ke0 concepts that this work established are precisely what target-controlled infusion systems and stanpumpR simulate. Sheiner also shaped drug-development methodology more broadly, articulating the distinction between "learning" and "confirming" trials. He received the ASCPT Oscar B. Hunter Award in 2004. Lewis Sheiner passed away in 2004.

*Key references:* Sheiner LB, Stanski DR, Vozeh S, Miller RD, Ham J. Simultaneous modeling of pharmacokinetics and pharmacodynamics: application to d-tubocurarine. Clin Pharmacol Ther. 1979;25(3):358–371. • Sheiner LB, Beal SL. Evaluation of methods for estimating population pharmacokinetics parameters. I. Michaelis-Menten model: routine clinical pharmacokinetic data. J Pharmacokinet Biopharm. 1980;8(6):553–571.

## University of Glasgow

**Gavin N. C. Kenny** — anesthesiologist; co-developer of the "Diprifusor" commercial TCI system and clinical implementer of the Marsh propofol model

Kenny, Emeritus Professor of Anaesthesia at the University of Glasgow, where he held the chair from 1996 to 2007, pioneered the clinical application of computer-controlled drug delivery, targeting a drug's concentration in the patient rather than merely its infusion rate. With Martin White he built a computerized propofol infusion system, and the underlying pharmacokinetic model — published with Brian Marsh and Neil Morton — became known as the Marsh model, a weight-proportional adaptation of the Gepts parameter set that remains pre-programmed in many TCI pumps. His research directly enabled the "Diprifusor," the first commercially available TCI system for propofol, launched by Zeneca in 1996.

*Key reference:* Marsh B, White M, Morton N, Kenny GNC. Pharmacokinetic model driven infusion of propofol in children. Br J Anaesth. 1991;67(1):41–48.

---

## University of Utah

**Talmage D. Egan** — anesthesiologist; remifentanil pharmacology, obesity PK, and novel opioids

Egan is a leading investigator in intravenous anesthetic pharmacology and total intravenous anesthesia (TIVA), best known for foundational clinical pharmacology of remifentanil, including one of the first detailed human pharmacokinetic characterizations and studies of its disposition in obesity. He co-authored the original remifentanil model-development work with Minto, Schnider, and Shafer, and later led development of a population pharmacokinetic model incorporating body mass to guide remifentanil dosing across the range from lean to obese patients. His work spans anesthetic drug interaction, pharmacokinetic modeling for TCI, and the preclinical/translational pharmacology of newer "soft" and novel opioids. He is Professor and served as Chair of Anesthesiology at the University of Utah School of Medicine.

*Key references:* Egan TD, Lemmens HJ, Fiset P, et al. The pharmacokinetics of the new short-acting opioid remifentanil (GI87084B) in healthy adult male volunteers. Anesthesiology. 1993;79(5):881–892. • Kim TK, Obara S, Egan TD, et al. Disposition of remifentanil in obesity: a new pharmacokinetic model incorporating the influence of body mass. Anesthesiology. 2017;126(6):1019–1032.

---

**Steven E. Kern** — engineer and pharmaceutical scientist, University of Utah (Pharmaceutics, Anesthesiology, and Bioengineering); opioid–hypnotic interaction and model-based drug delivery (later Novartis and the Bill & Melinda Gates Foundation)

Steven Kern is a bioengineer and clinical pharmacologist who spent roughly fifteen years on the faculty at the University of Utah, with appointments spanning Pharmaceutics, Anesthesiology, and Bioengineering. Trained in engineering (mechanical engineering, Cornell; bioengineering, Penn State and Utah), he applied a strongly quantitative, model-based approach to anesthetic PK/PD, working alongside the Utah anesthesia group — notably Talmage D. Egan and, in closed-loop/model-based delivery work, Dwayne Westenskow. His research emphasized effect-site modeling, opioid–hypnotic synergy, and the translation of interaction models into model-based and closed-loop drug delivery.

Kern is best known in this area for a volunteer study, published back-to-back with Bouillon's paper in the same 2004 issue of Anesthesiology, that used a response surface to characterize the propofol–remifentanil pharmacodynamic interaction across a complete range of clinically relevant concentrations. Using surrogate noxious stimuli (algometry, tetany), sedation, and laryngoscopy as endpoints, the analysis quantified pronounced synergy between the two drugs, reinforcing the rationale for combining a hypnotic and an opioid at reduced individual concentrations. He later moved into industry (pharmacology modeling, including at Novartis, Basel) and then to global health, serving in quantitative-sciences leadership at the Bill & Melinda Gates Foundation.

*Key reference:* Kern SE, Xie G, White JL, Egan TD. A response surface analysis of propofol–remifentanil pharmacodynamic interaction in volunteers. Anesthesiology. 2004;100(6):1373–1381.

---

**Theodore H. "Ted" Stanley** — professor of anesthesiology, University of Utah; high-dose opioid anesthesia and oral transmucosal fentanyl

Stanley trained in Cleveland under Willem Kolff and followed him to the University of Utah, where he spent his entire career and contributed to the artificial-heart program that produced the first permanent implant in 1982. His central contribution to anesthesia was the systematic development of high-dose opioid anesthesia for cardiac surgery. With Lynn Webster he characterized the anesthetic requirements and cardiovascular effects of fentanyl–oxygen and fentanyl–diazepam–oxygen anesthesia in patients undergoing mitral valve replacement, quantifying the doses required for surgical anesthesia and showing that fentanyl alone preserved stroke volume and cardiac output while the addition of diazepam depressed them. That dose–requirement and drug-interaction work helped displace high-dose morphine as the standard technique for hemodynamically fragile patients. Collaborating with Paul Janssen of Janssen Pharmaceutica, Stanley was instrumental in bringing the fentanyl family of opioids — fentanyl, sufentanil, and alfentanil — into anesthetic practice, a history he later recounted in his retrospective "The fentanyl story."

Observing that orally administered fentanyl produced effects far faster than gastric absorption could explain, Stanley and colleagues inferred direct uptake across the oral mucosa and developed oral transmucosal fentanyl citrate (OTFC), a fentanyl-containing lozenge on a handle, first as premedication for children and preoperative patients and then, through Anesta Corp. — the Salt Lake City company he co-founded with William Moeller — as the breakthrough-cancer-pain product Actiq. The pharmacokinetics of that route were characterized in a study with Streisand, Varvel, Donald Stanski, and Michael Ashburn, which measured the absorbed fraction and absolute bioavailability of OTFC against intravenous fentanyl and demonstrated that a substantial portion is taken up transmucosally, bypassing first-pass hepatic extraction. That characterization made non-intravenous fentanyl delivery pharmacokinetically predictable, and it is a direct antecedent of the oral and transmucosal absorption models used in simulators such as stanpumpR.

For decades Stanley directed the Utah Postgraduate Course in Anesthesiology, editing its proceedings as a long-running book series with W. Clayton Petty. The meeting is now held annually as the Theodore H. Stanley Annual Update in Anesthesiology. Ted Stanley passed away in 2017.

*Key references:* Stanley TH, Webster LR. Anesthetic requirements and cardiovascular effects of fentanyl-oxygen and fentanyl-diazepam-oxygen anesthesia in man. Anesth Analg. 1978;57(4):411–416. • Streisand JB, Varvel JR, Stanski DR, Le Maire L, Ashburn MA, Hague BI, et al. Absorption and bioavailability of oral transmucosal fentanyl citrate. Anesthesiology. 1991;75(2):223–229.

---

**Dwayne R. Westenskow** — bioengineer; professor of anesthesiology and bioengineering; automated (closed-loop) drug delivery, anesthesia monitoring, and patient safety

Westenskow built one of the longest-running academic programs in automated anesthesia delivery and monitoring. Beginning in the 1970s with oxygen-consumption measurement during anesthesia, he turned to feedback control in 1977 and, over the following decades, demonstrated closed-loop controllers for volatile-anesthetic and respiratory-gas delivery, blood pressure (e.g., nitroprusside infusion), neuromuscular blockade, mechanical ventilation, and fluid resuscitation — showing that automatic controllers could match expert clinicians. His group integrated these controllers into the concept of an automated "anesthesia workstation," and he made major contributions to intelligent alarms, artificial-neural-network signal processing, and noninvasive monitoring (including CO2-rebreathing cardiac output). Much of this work connects the pharmacokinetic/pharmacodynamic modeling of anesthetics to the engineering of the sensors and controllers needed to deliver them safely in real time.

*Key reference:* Westenskow DR, Wallroth CF. Closed-loop control for anesthesia breathing systems. J Clin Monit. 1990;6(3):249–256.

---

## Vrije Universiteit Brussel (VUB), Belgium

**Frederic Camu** — emeritus professor and long-time chair of anesthesiology, Vrije Universiteit Brussel

Frederic Camu was a Belgian anesthesiologist who led the Department of Anesthesiology at the Vrije Universiteit Brussel (VUB) for many years and built a research program centered on the clinical pharmacology of intravenous anesthetics, opioids, and analgesics — including their effects on hemodynamics, respiratory control, and acute nociception. Working at Brussels in the mid-1980s, he collaborated with Elisabeth Gepts on the human disposition studies of propofol that would become foundational to modern target-controlled infusion (TCI).

Camu was a co-author of the 1987 Gepts et al. constant-rate infusion study, whose three-compartment parameter set was later adapted by Marsh, White, Morton, and Kenny into the "Marsh" model used in the Diprifusor and many subsequent TCI systems, and which Coetzee and colleagues found to perform well when they assessed the predictive accuracy of three published propofol parameter sets. Frederic Camu passed away in 2024.

*Key reference:* Gepts E, Camu F, Cockshott ID, Douglas EJ. Disposition of propofol administered as constant rate intravenous infusions in humans. Anesth Analg. 1987;66(12):1256–1263.

---

**Elisabeth Gepts** — clinical-pharmacology researcher in anesthesiology; source of the propofol disposition dataset underlying the Marsh model

Elisabeth Gepts (published as "Gepts E") was a Brussels-based clinical pharmacology and anesthesiology researcher whose 1987 study of propofol disposition during constant-rate intravenous infusion provided the parameter estimates that underpin one of the most widely deployed pharmacokinetic models in anesthesia. In that work she and colleagues administered propofol at 3, 6, and 9 mg·kg⁻¹·hr⁻¹ to surgical patients under regional anesthesia, sampled arterial blood during and after infusion, and fitted the data to a three-compartment open mammillary model with central elimination — establishing the volumes and clearances that describe propofol disposition in humans.

That dataset, produced through the Camu–Gepts collaboration at the Vrije Universiteit Brussel, was subsequently adapted by Marsh, White, Morton, and Kenny (1991) into the weight-proportional "Marsh" model implemented in the AstraZeneca Diprifusor and in numerous later TCI pumps; it also served as a reference point in Coetzee et al.'s comparative evaluations of propofol PK models. Gepts is credited with later helping to recover the original source data underlying these parameters.

*Key reference:* Gepts E, Camu F, Cockshott ID, Douglas EJ. Disposition of propofol administered as constant rate intravenous infusions in humans. Anesth Analg. 1987;66(12):1256–1263.

---

## Wake Forest University School of Medicine

**James C. Eisenach** — anesthesiologist and pain pharmacologist, Wake Forest University School of Medicine; oxytocin pharmacokinetics, spinal analgesic pharmacology, and the transition from acute to chronic pain

James C. Eisenach has spent his faculty career in the Department of Anesthesiology at Wake Forest University School of Medicine in Winston-Salem, North Carolina. He served as Editor-in-Chief of *Anesthesiology* from 2007 to 2016, immediately preceding Evan D. Kharasch, and served as President and Chief Executive Officer of the Foundation for Anesthesia Education and Research from 2016 to 2023.

Eisenach is the senior author of the study that supplies stanpumpR's oxytocin model. Oxytocin had long been given clinically without a well-characterized human disposition model, in part because measuring the peptide at endogenous concentrations is analytically difficult. Working with Steven L. Shafer, Douglas Ririe, and colleagues, he studied intravenous and intranasal oxytocin in nonpregnant adults and found that the plasma pharmacokinetics of the intravenous drug were well described by a two-compartment model (0% bias, 18% median inaccuracy) — a compact, closed-form-friendly result of exactly the kind a simulator needs. The intranasal route behaved very differently: bioavailability was approximately 0.7%, with substantially greater between-subject variability, which the authors argued could partly explain the inconsistent reports of behavioral and analgesic efficacy in the large intranasal-oxytocin literature. The paper includes a simulator intended to guide dosing in future trials. His oxytocin program treats the peptide as an analgesic acting at the spinal cord rather than as a uterotonic: he carried intrathecal oxytocin from preclinical toxicology in rats and dogs through a Phase 1 human safety assessment and into randomized trials in hip arthroplasty and in neuropathic pain.

His earlier and larger body of work established much of the pharmacology of spinal and epidural analgesia. He was a central figure in the clinical development of epidural and intrathecal clonidine and related alpha-2 adrenergic agonists, synthesizing a decade of that literature in a widely cited 1996 review. In parallel he pursued cholinergic spinal analgesia, taking intrathecal neostigmine from preclinical safety screening through Phase 1 human assessment and into trials of labor analgesia, on the rationale that inhibiting spinal acetylcholinesterase amplifies an endogenous analgesic system engaged by alpha-2 agonists. Much of this work was done in the obstetric setting, and it led him toward the mechanisms of the transition from acute to chronic pain after surgery — including the observation that pregnancy and the puerperium alter spinal plasticity after nerve injury through oxytocinergic signaling, the finding that connects his obstetric anesthesia origins to the oxytocin program above.

*Key references:* Eisenach JC, De Kock M, Klimscha W. alpha(2)-adrenergic agonists for regional anesthesia. A clinical review of clonidine (1984–1995). Anesthesiology. 1996;85(3):655–674. • Shafer SL, Ririe DG, Miller S, Curry RS, Hsu DT, Sullivan GM, Eisenach JC. Plasma pharmacokinetics of intravenous and intranasal oxytocin in nonpregnant adults. Br J Anaesth. 2025;134(5):1513–1522.
